1. Overview

Note on substitution: the reference chapter uses an annual “Singapore Residents by Planning Area/Subzone, Age Group, Sex and Type of Dwelling” release, which has since been retired from data.gov.sg’s catalogue (it no longer turns up under its old file name respopagesextod, or under a search for its own title). The nearest dataset still published at subzone level is the Census of Population 2020 table used here. It has a different shape to the retired series: it comes as one wide table with a single Number column that mixes planning-area subtotal rows (suffixed - Total) with subzone rows, rather than separate PA and SZ columns, so the wrangling below spells out the extra reshaping step that the original exercise didn’t need. It also reuses the Master Plan 2014 boundary from Part 01 rather than 2019, so both parts of this exercise share the same base map.

title: Choropleth Mapping with R
text:
4. Importing and Preparing the Data

4.1 Geospatial data
Re-importing the same Master Plan 2014 subzone boundary used in Part 01. Each exercise page runs as its own self-contained R session, so the object isn’t carried over automatically:

mpsz <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial/MasterPlan2014SubzoneBoundaryNoSea.geojson") %>%
  st_transform(crs = 3414)

Reading layer `MP14_SUBZONE_NO_SEA_PL' from data source 
  `/Users/jedidiahasaf/Downloads/School/ISSS626/coursework-website/Hands-on_Ex/Hands-on_Ex01/data/geospatial/MasterPlan2014SubzoneBoundaryNoSea.geojson' 
  using driver `GeoJSON'
Simple feature collection with 323 features and 13 fields
Geometry type: MULTIPOLYGON
Dimension:     XY
Bounding box:  xmin: 103.6057 ymin: 1.158699 xmax: 104.0885 ymax: 1.470775
Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84




4.2 Aspatial data

popdata <- read_csv("data/aspatial/respop2020.csv", na = "-")

The na = "-" argument matters here: SingStat suppresses small subzone counts with a literal -, and without telling read_csv() to treat that as a missing value, every numeric column in the table gets silently parsed as text.


4.3 Data wrangling
The Number column mixes two kinds of row: planning-area subtotals, named like "Ang Mo Kio - Total", and the individual subzone rows that follow each one. A forward-fill turns that into a proper PA column before the subtotal rows are dropped:

pop_sz <- popdata %>%
  filter(Number != "Total") %>%
  mutate(PA = if_else(str_detect(Number, "-\\s*Total$"),
                       str_remove(Number, "-\\s*Total$") %>% str_trim(),
                       NA_character_)) %>%
  fill(PA, .direction = "down") %>%
  filter(!str_detect(Number, "-\\s*Total$")) %>%
  rename(SZ = Number)







NoteData quality quirk



One planning-area subtotal row breaks the " - Total" pattern: Changi is written as "Changi- Total", with no space before the dash, while every other area uses "Changi Bay - Total" with a space. The regex above (-\s*Total$) allows for zero or more spaces so it still catches it. A plain " - Total$" match would have let "Changi- Total" slip through as if it were a subzone named "Changi- Total", similar in spirit to the YISHUN/Yishun case-mismatch flagged in the KNIME Data Analytics Lab exercise.


Computing the young / economically active / aged breakdown and the dependency ratio:

pop_sz <- pop_sz %>%
  mutate(
    YOUNG = Total_0_4 + Total_5_9 + Total_10_14 + Total_15_19 + Total_20_24,
    `ECONOMY ACTIVE` = Total_25_29 + Total_30_34 + Total_35_39 + Total_40_44 +
      Total_45_49 + Total_50_54 + Total_55_59 + Total_60_64,
    AGED = Total_65_69 + Total_70_74 + Total_75_79 + Total_80_84 + Total_85_89 +
      Total_90andOver,
    TOTAL = Total_Total,
    DEPENDENCY = (YOUNG + AGED) / `ECONOMY ACTIVE`
  ) %>%
  select(PA, SZ, YOUNG, `ECONOMY ACTIVE`, AGED, TOTAL, DEPENDENCY) %>%
  mutate(SZ = toupper(SZ), PA = toupper(PA)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(`ECONOMY ACTIVE`), `ECONOMY ACTIVE` > 0)

nrow(pop_sz)

[1] 224




4.4 Joining geospatial and aspatial data

mpsz_pop2020 <- left_join(mpsz, pop_sz, by = c("SUBZONE_N" = "SZ"))
sum(!is.na(mpsz_pop2020$DEPENDENCY))

[1] 201


201 of 323 subzones get a dependency ratio. The rest (industrial estates, parks, water catchment areas, and a handful of 2014-vs-2020 subzone boundary renames) have no resident population in the 2020 Census and are left as NA rather than dropped, so the map below shows them un-shaded instead of silently disappearing.

text:
5. Choropleth Mapping with tmap

5.1 A quick map with qtm()

tmap_mode("plot")
qtm(shp = mpsz_pop2020, fill = "DEPENDENCY")










5.2 A fuller map built from tmap’s elements

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_title("Dependency ratio by planning subzone, Singapore") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(alpha = 0.2) +
  tm_credits(
    "Source: Master Plan 2014 Subzone Boundary (URA) and Census of Population 2020 (SingStat)",
    position = c("left", "bottom"))










5.3 Comparing classification methods
DIY: prepare choropleth maps using different classification methods and compare.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Quantile")









tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "equal", n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Equal interval")









tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "jenks", n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Jenks natural breaks")








Quantile forces the same number of subzones into every bucket, which spreads colour evenly across the map regardless of how the underlying values are actually distributed. It is the most visually “balanced” of the three but can group very different dependency ratios into one class if the data clusters tightly. Equal interval slices the value range into five equal-width bands; because most subzones sit in a fairly narrow band, that concentrates almost every subzone into one or two classes and leaves the rest of the legend almost empty. Jenks looks for natural gaps in the data itself, so the class breaks land where the dependency ratio actually jumps, which here sits closer to quantile than to equal interval.


5.4 Comparing number of classes
DIY: prepare choropleth maps using the same classification method but with 2, 6, 10, and 20 classes, and compare.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 2)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("n = 2")









tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 6)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("n = 6")









tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 10)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("n = 10")









tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 20)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("n = 20")








At n = 2 the map only distinguishes “below median” from “above median” dependency, which hides all the variation within each half. Pushing up to n = 10 or n = 20 starts creating classes so narrow that neighbouring subzones with almost identical ratios get visibly different colours, which reads as more precision than the data actually supports. With only 201 subzones, 20 quantile bins means roughly 10 subzones per class, each one a razor-thin slice of the value range. Something in the 5–6 range is where the map still shows a clear spatial pattern without either flattening the variation or manufacturing false precision.

title: Choropleth Mapping with R
text:
8. Reflections
The biggest difference from the reference chapter was upstream of any mapping code: the exact population dataset it names has been retired, so getting from “a CSV with an age/sex breakdown” to “one row per subzone with a dependency ratio” took real wrangling rather than a straight read-and-join. The Number column mixing planning-area subtotals with subzone rows, - used for suppressed counts, and the one inconsistent "Changi- Total" label were all things I only found by actually inspecting the output at each step rather than assuming the code from the reference chapter would apply unchanged. Once the join was right, the tmap classification and class-count comparisons were the part that most changed how I’d read a choropleth map going forward. The classification method and the number of classes are both editorial choices, not neutral defaults, and they can make the same underlying data look like a strong spatial pattern or a fairly flat one.

title: Second-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis
text:
R spatstat G / F / K / L Monte Carlo
This is the second of the two Spatial Point Patterns Analysis readings for Hands-on Exercise 2: 2nd Order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis Methods. The first-order methods are in Part 01.

title: Second-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis
text:
1. Overview
First-order analysis asked how intensity varies across space. Second-order analysis asks a different question: do the events interact? Given the number of points present, are they closer together than chance would produce (attraction / clustering), further apart (inhibition / regularity), or indistinguishable from random?
Four distance-based functions answer this at a range of scales:








Function
Measures
Clustered when




G
distance from each event to its nearest event
curve rises above the CSR envelope


F
distance from random locations to the nearest event
curve falls below the CSR envelope


K
cumulative count of events within distance r
curve rises above the envelope


L
K, variance-stabilised to a flat zero line
curve rises above zero



Each is tested against a Monte Carlo envelope built from simulated CSR patterns. That envelope is the whole point: a raw G or K curve on its own tells me nothing, because almost every real pattern deviates somewhat from the theoretical CSR line.

text:

4. Data Import and Preparation
Repeating the Part 01 preparation so this page stands on its own, because each Quarto page is its own R session.

mpsz_sf <- st_read("data/geospatial/MasterPlan2019SubzoneBoundaryNoSea.geojson",
                   quiet = TRUE) %>%
  st_transform(crs = 3414)

childcare_sf <- st_read("data/geospatial/ChildCareServices.geojson",
                        quiet = TRUE) %>%
  st_transform(crs = 3414)


set.seed(1234)
childcare_ppp <- as.ppp(childcare_sf)
childcare_ppp_jit <- rjitter(childcare_ppp, retry = TRUE, nsim = 1, drop = TRUE)
any(duplicated(childcare_ppp_jit))

Without it the exact distance at which each observed curve crosses its envelope shifts by a few tens of metres on every rebuild, which makes any number I quote in the text wrong the next time the site is deployed.

section: 5. A Note on the Hypotheses and the Number of Simulations
text:
5. A Note on the Hypotheses and the Number of Simulations
For every test below:
\(H_0\): the distribution of childcare centres in the study area is randomly distributed. \(H_1\): the distribution is not randomly distributed.
\(H_0\) is rejected at the 95% level if the observed curve leaves the envelope built from the simulated CSR patterns.
On nsim. The reference chapter uses nsim = 999. I use nsim = 99 throughout this page. With 99 simulations the envelope is the pointwise minimum and maximum of the simulations, which corresponds to a two-sided significance level of 2/(99+1) = 0.02, comfortably inside the 0.05 I am testing at, and it keeps this page rendering in seconds rather than minutes, which matters because the site is rebuilt on every deploy. Where the observed curve leaves the envelope below it does so by a wide margin rather than grazing the edge, so the extra simulations would not change the reading. A marginal result would be a reason to raise nsim, and I would.

ImportantF and G point in opposite directions, and that is correct



G above the envelope and F below the envelope look like contradictory results but are the same finding stated twice: G is measured from events, F from empty space. A clustered pattern has short event-to-event distances (G up) and large voids between clusters (F down). If both pointed the same way, one of them would be wrong.
The computed table in section 10 confirms this holds in both study areas: G leaves its envelope upward, F leaves its envelope downward, and K and L leave theirs upward. Four statistics built on different distance definitions all reject CSR, consistently.
One caveat I want on the record. An earlier run of this page, before I fixed the seed, produced an F-function for Choa Chu Kang that never left its envelope at all, the opposite significance verdict from the one shown here. With only 74 points and 99 simulations, F in Choa Chu Kang is marginal enough that the answer moved with the simulation draw. G, K and L did not move. That is the concrete reason the seed is now fixed at the top of this page, and a warning against quoting a borderline Monte Carlo result as though it were stable. If this were assessed work with consequences I would raise nsim for F specifically rather than rely on a single draw.

10. Where Each Curve Leaves Its Envelope
Reading significance off eight plots by eye is unreliable, so I compute it directly. For G, K and L a departure above the upper envelope indicates clustering; for F a departure below the lower envelope does.

crossing <- function(env, side) {
  d <- if (side == "above") env$r[env$obs > env$hi] else env$r[env$obs < env$lo]
  d <- d[!is.na(d)]
  if (length(d) == 0) "never leaves envelope"
  else paste0(round(min(d)), "-", round(max(d)), " m")
}

section: 11. What I Take From This Exercise
text:
11. What I Take From This Exercise
All four functions agree. In both Choa Chu Kang and Tampines, G, K and L rise above their envelopes and F falls below its own. Four different statistics, built on different distance definitions, all rejecting complete spatial randomness in the same direction. Childcare centres in both towns are clustered.
The agreement is firmer in Tampines than in Choa Chu Kang. Tampines has 117 points to Choa Chu Kang’s 74, its curves leave the envelopes earlier and stay outside them longer, and its F result was stable across simulation draws where Choa Chu Kang’s was not.
Scale is the real finding. What matters is not that the curves leave the envelope but over what range, and the table in section 10 makes two things obvious. First, K departs over a far wider range than G in both areas, which is unsurprising since K counts all neighbours rather than only the nearest, so it detects clustering that nearest-neighbour distances alone miss. Second, the two towns cluster at genuinely different scales: Tampines stays outside its K envelope well past a kilometre, while Choa Chu Kang returns inside it several hundred metres earlier. Those are two different spatial processes, and calling both simply “clustered” would throw the distinction away. A first-order KDE could not have told me any of this, because KDE has no notion of scale-dependent interaction.
What I got wrong, twice. First I read the F-function plot as contradicting the G-function plot and assumed I had mis-specified the edge correction. The two functions are supposed to point in opposite directions for a clustered pattern; writing out what each one measures from (events for G, empty space for F) fixed that.
The second mistake was the instructive one. I wrote up the significance verdicts from reading the plots, then built the table in section 10 to compute them properly, and the F result for Choa Chu Kang came out differently from what I had written. Chasing it down, the cause was not a coding error but an unfixed random seed: F in that area is close enough to its envelope that the verdict moved between simulation runs. Two lessons out of one bug: compute the crossing points rather than eyeballing them, and fix the seed before writing any sentence that depends on a Monte Carlo result.
Limitation, again. Every test here compares the observed pattern to complete spatial randomness within the planning area polygon. But a childcare centre cannot be sited in a canal, a cemetery, a reservoir or an expressway interchange, and a meaningful share of both study areas is exactly that. The CSR null is therefore slightly too generous, and some of the measured “clustering” is really just “buildings are where buildings can be”. The honest fix is an inhomogeneous null (Kinhom, Linhom) fitted to a population or land-use covariate rather than a homogeneous CSR, which is where I would take this next.
This is not a hypothetical worry. In Hands-on Exercise 3 I run the network-constrained equivalent of the K-function on Punggol, where the null only scatters simulated points along roads rather than anywhere inside the polygon, and the result flips from clustering to regularity. Some of what this page measures as clustering is the shape of the study area, not the behaviour of childcare operators.

title: Spatial Weights and Applications
text:
1. Overview
Everything in Exercises 2 and 3 treated space as distance between points. This exercise switches to areal data, meaning polygons with values attached, where the question is no longer “how far apart are these events” but “which regions are neighbours, and how much should each neighbour count?”
That is what a spatial weights matrix encodes. It is the object that every subsequent technique in the course depends on: spatial autocorrelation, clustering, and geographically weighted regression all take a weights matrix as input. Getting it wrong quietly invalidates everything downstream, which is why a whole exercise is spent on it.
By the end I should be able to compute contiguity weights, distance-based weights, inverse-distance weights, row-standardise them, and use them to derive spatially lagged variables.

6. Computing Contiguity Spatial Weights
Contiguity weights define neighbours by shared boundaries. The two standard rules are named after chess moves:

Queen: regions are neighbours if they share any boundary point, edge or corner.
Rook: regions are neighbours only if they share an edge.

text:
7. Computing Distance-based Neighbours
Contiguity ignores distance entirely: a shared border counts the same whether the two county centres are 20 km or 200 km apart. Distance-based weights take the opposite view.

7.1 Determining the Cut-off Distance
The cut-off must be large enough that no county is left with zero neighbours. The standard approach is to find the distance to each county’s first nearest neighbour and take the maximum of those.

k1 <- knn2nb(knearneigh(coords))
k1dists <- unlist(nbdists(k1, coords, longlat = TRUE))
summary(k1dists)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  24.79   32.56   38.00   39.07   44.52   61.81 








ImportantThe mistake that cost me this section



My first attempt passed the output of st_centroid() straight into knearneigh(), an sfc object rather than a coordinate matrix, and got a maximum first-neighbour distance of 0.6 instead of 61.8. The longlat = TRUE argument was silently overridden, so spdep measured in degrees of latitude and longitude as though they were planar units. A 62-unit cut-off then made every county a neighbour of every other county, and the fixed-distance matrix came out with 87 links per county instead of about 4.
What makes this dangerous is that it does not error. It produces a perfectly well-formed weights matrix that is completely wrong, and every statistic computed from it afterwards would have been wrong too, with nothing to indicate a problem. The lesson: pass st_coordinates() output, and sanity-check that the distances come back in plausible kilometres before using them.


The maximum first-nearest-neighbour distance is about 62 km, so every county is guaranteed at least one neighbour at that cut-off.

Every county now has exactly six neighbours. That guarantees no isolates and a balanced weights matrix, but it forces a relationship where none may exist: a remote western county gets six neighbours even if the nearest is far away and arguably irrelevant.
The fixed-distance matrix is the honest one about geography and the dishonest one about balance; the adaptive matrix is the reverse. Neither is correct in the abstract. What matters is stating which was used and why, because the choice propagates into every subsequent result.

section: 11. My Own Exploration: Does the Choice of Weights Matrix Actually Matter?
text:
11. My Own Exploration: Does the Choice of Weights Matrix Actually Matter?
Everything above follows the reference chapter. This section does not. Writing section 10 left me with a question the exercise never asks: I had just built five different definitions of “neighbour” from one unchanged shapefile, and I had no idea whether that choice changes any answer or is merely bookkeeping. Rather than assert it matters, I decided to measure it.
The test is simple. Compute the spatially lagged GDP per capita under every weighting scheme, then correlate the resulting vectors. If the correlations are near 1, the choice is cosmetic. If they are not, every downstream statistic inherits the choice.

11.1 Building All Five Schemes

wm_d62_e  <- dnearneigh(coords, 0, 62, longlat = TRUE)
knn6_e    <- knn2nb(knearneigh(coords, k = 6))
dist_e    <- nbdists(wm_q, coords, longlat = TRUE)
ids_e     <- lapply(dist_e, function(x) 1 / x)

lagged <- data.frame(
  Queen     = lag.listw(nb2listw(wm_q,    style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE), hunan$GDPPC),
  Rook      = lag.listw(nb2listw(wm_r,    style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE), hunan$GDPPC),
  Fixed62   = lag.listw(nb2listw(wm_d62_e,style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE), hunan$GDPPC,
                        zero.policy = TRUE),
  Adaptive6 = lag.listw(nb2listw(knn6_e,  style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE), hunan$GDPPC),
  IDW       = lag.listw(nb2listw(wm_q, glist = ids_e, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE),
                        hunan$GDPPC)
)



11.2 How Connected Is Each Scheme?

data.frame(
  Scheme   = c("Queen", "Rook", "Fixed 62 km", "Adaptive k=6"),
  Links    = c(sum(card(wm_q)), sum(card(wm_r)), sum(card(wm_d62_e)), sum(card(knn6_e))),

               sum(card(wm_d62_e) == 0), sum(card(knn6_e) == 0))
)

      main = "Lagged GDPPC under five weighting schemes")














ImportantThe answer, and it is not uniform



The correlations split the five schemes into two camps.
Queen and rook are effectively the same thing here. They correlate at 0.998. I had already guessed this in section 6.2 from the link counts, but guessing and measuring are different, and now I can say it rather than hedge it.
Contiguity and distance are not the same thing at all. Queen against the fixed 62 km band correlates at only 0.875. That is a real divergence. Roughly a quarter of the variance in one lagged variable is unexplained by the other, from identical input data, purely because of how I defined “neighbour”.
So the honest summary is that the queen/rook decision is safe to make casually, and the contiguity/distance decision is not. Those two choices are presented side by side in the chapter as though they were the same kind of decision. They are not.




11.4 Which Counties Disagree Most?
An average hides where the disagreement lives, so I looked at the individual counties where queen contiguity and adaptive k=6 diverge most.

Before asserting a pattern from the top eight, I tested it across all 88 counties.

  `Mean disagreement %` = round(c(mean(pct_diff[card(wm_q) <= 3]),

                                  mean(pct_diff[card(wm_q) >= 7])), 1),
  check.names = FALSE

3        7 or more       18                 7.2

cor(card(wm_q), pct_diff)

[1] -0.1795046








NoteWhere the disagreement concentrates, and how strong that pattern really is



My first reading of the top-eight table was that poorly connected counties disagree most. Longshan is the worst case at about 32% and has only 3 queen neighbours, which fits neatly.
Then I checked it properly, and the neat story is only partly true. Counties with 3 or fewer neighbours do disagree more on average (10.4% against roughly 7.2% for everyone else), but the correlation between neighbour count and disagreement is only about -0.18. That is a weak tendency, not a rule. Taojiang sits second in the table with a 25% gap and has 7 neighbours, which the story does not explain at all.
The mechanism I can defend is narrower than the one I first reached for. If a county has three contiguous neighbours and adaptive weighting forces it to six, three non-touching counties each receive a sixth of the weight, which can move the average a long way. That explains Longshan. It does not explain Taojiang, where something else is going on, most likely a neighbour with an extreme GDPPC entering or leaving the set.
What I take from this is less about Hunan than about my own habit. I had the explanation written before I had the correlation, and the correlation turned out to be 0.18 rather than the 0.6 or 0.7 my confident phrasing implied. Ranking a table by one column and reading a cause off the top rows is a good way to generate a hypothesis and a bad way to confirm one.

title: Spatial Weights and Applications
section: 12. What I Take From This Exercise
text:
12. What I Take From This Exercise
The weights matrix is a modelling assumption, not a data property. Nothing in the Hunan shapefile tells me whether two counties are neighbours. Queen or rook, 62 km or 6 nearest neighbours, binary or inverse-distance, row-standardised or not. Each is a decision I make, and each produces a different matrix from identical data. Every autocorrelation statistic and spatial regression later in the course inherits whichever one I pick. This exercise is not really about spdep syntax; it is about the fact that a large part of a spatial analysis is decided before any statistic is computed.
The silent-failure lesson. The sfc-versus-matrix mistake in section 7.1 is the one I will actually remember. It did not throw an error, it did not produce an obviously absurd map, and it yielded a valid weights object. It was simply measuring degrees and calling them kilometres. The only thing that caught it was noticing that a first-nearest-neighbour distance of 0.6 km between Chinese counties is impossible. Unit plausibility checks are not busywork; here they were the only line of defence.
Averages versus sums matter more than they look. The four lag definitions in section 10 produce visibly different maps from the same variable and the same neighbour list. The binary-sum versions are partly just a map of how many neighbours each county has, which is a property of the geography rather than of GDP. Row standardisation removes that artefact, which is why it is the sensible default for comparing across regions of uneven connectivity.
Connecting forward. The row-standardised queen contiguity matrix built here is the direct input to Moran’s I and Geary’s C in the next exercise. Section 11 gives me a concrete expectation to carry into that: switching between queen and rook should barely move Moran’s I, while switching from contiguity to a distance band plausibly could. I intend to run the autocorrelation statistic under at least two weighting schemes rather than report a single number as though the matrix behind it were a fact about Hunan instead of a decision I made.

title: Network Constrained Spatial Point Patterns Analysis
text:
1. Overview
Everything in Hands-on Exercise 2 assumed events could fall anywhere on a two-dimensional plane, and measured distance as the straight line between them. For childcare centres that assumption is wrong in a specific way: a centre sits on a street, a parent walks along streets, and two centres on opposite banks of Punggol Waterway are 80 metres apart in Euclidean terms and roughly a kilometre apart in walking terms.
Network constrained SPPA fixes that by confining both the events and the distance metric to the network itself. This exercise uses spNetwork to:

derive a network kernel density estimate (NKDE), and
perform network-constrained G- and K-function analysis.

The study area is Punggol.

text:
6. Network KDE Analysis

6.1 Preparing the Lixels
A kernel density estimate on a network is evaluated along the network, not over a grid. The first step is to cut the network into lixels, or line pixels, of roughly equal length.

lixels <- lixelize_lines(network,
                         700,
                         mindist = 375)
nrow(lixels)

[1] 2645


The 700m target length with a 375m minimum means any leftover segment shorter than 375m is merged into the previous lixel rather than left as a stub. The count barely changes from the original 2,642 segments, which tells me most Punggol road segments were already shorter than 700m. This is a dense residential network, not a highway corridor.


6.2 Generating Line Centre Points

samples <- lines_center(lixels)
nrow(samples)

[1] 2645


These centre points are where the density will actually be evaluated. Note they are the centre of each lixel by line length, not the geometric centroid, so they always fall on the line even where it bends.


6.3 Performing NKDE

densities <- nkde(network,
                  events = childcare,
                  w = rep(1, nrow(childcare)),
                  samples = samples,
                  kernel_name = "quartic",
                  bw = 300,
                  div = "bw",
                  method = "simple",
                  digits = 1,
                  tol = 1,
                  grid_shape = c(1, 1),
                  max_depth = 8,
                  agg = 5,
                  sparse = TRUE,
                  verbose = FALSE)

A note on the arguments that actually change the answer:

kernel_name = "quartic" sets the kernel shape. spNetwork also offers triangle, gaussian, tricube, cosine, epanechnikov and uniform.
bw = 300 is the bandwidth, in metres along the network. This is the single most consequential choice here.
method = "simple" is the simplest of the three NKDE variants. It treats network distance as a straight replacement for Euclidean distance in the kernel. It is fast and intuitive, but it is not a true density: the values do not integrate to the number of events, because mass is duplicated at every intersection. "discontinuous" and "continuous" correct that at increasing computational cost.

Attaching the computed densities and rescaling from events-per-metre to events-per-kilometre so the legend is readable:

samples$density <- densities
lixels$density  <- densities

samples$density <- samples$density * 1000
lixels$density  <- lixels$density * 1000


summary(lixels$density)

0.000000 0.000000 0.001424 0.003787 0.007430 0.024046

  tm_lines(col = "density",
           col.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", values = "viridis"),
           col.legend = tm_legend(title = "Density (events/km)"),
           lwd = 1.5) +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE)














NoteWhat the NKDE map shows that a planar KDE would not



The high-density road segments are not a blob in the middle of Punggol. They are specific stretches, the roads threading the HDB precincts either side of Punggol Field and Punggol Central, while the roads along the waterway and the LRT viaduct run cold despite being geometrically close to plenty of centres. A planar KDE would smear density straight across the waterway and report a hotspot in the middle of the water, which is exactly the artefact this method exists to avoid.

7. Network Constrained G- and K-Function Analysis
The same complete spatial randomness question as Hands-on Exercise 2 Part 02, but with randomness defined on the network: the simulated points are scattered along the road network rather than across the plane.
\(H_0\): the observed spatial point events are uniformly distributed over the street network in Punggol. \(H_1\): the observed spatial point events are not uniformly distributed over the street network.
The test is at the 95% confidence interval, with the null rejected if the observed curve leaves the simulated envelope.

set.seed(1234)
kfun_childcare <- kfunctions(network,
                             childcare,
                             start = 0,
                             end = 1000,
                             step = 50,
                             width = 50,
                             nsim = 50,
                             resolution = 50,
                             verbose = FALSE,
                             conf_int = 0.05)


7.1 The K-Function Result

kfun_childcare$plotk










7.2 The G-Function Result

kfun_childcare$plotg








Reading the direction off the plots by eye is unreliable, so I compute where the observed curve actually leaves the simulated envelope:

v <- kfun_childcare$values

rng <- function(d) {
  if (length(d) == 0) {
    "never leaves envelope"
  } else {
    paste0(min(d), "-", max(d), " m")
  }
}

data.frame(
  Function = c("Network K", "Network K", "Network G", "Network G"),
  Side = c("above upper (clustered)", "below lower (regular)",
           "above upper (clustered)", "below lower (regular)"),
  Range = c(rng(v$distances[v$obs_k > v$upper_k & v$distances > 0]),
            rng(v$distances[v$obs_k < v$lower_k]),
            rng(v$distances[v$obs_g > v$upper_g & v$distances > 0]),
            rng(v$distances[v$obs_g < v$lower_g]))
)

   Function                    Side                 Range
1 Network K above upper (clustered) never leaves envelope
2 Network K   below lower (regular)             150-550 m
3 Network G above upper (clustered) never leaves envelope
4 Network G   below lower (regular)             150-500 m








ImportantConclusion of the test, and it is not what I expected



The observed curves leave the envelope on the lower side, not the upper one. Fewer centres fall within a few hundred network metres of each other than complete spatial randomness along the network would produce.
I reject the null hypothesis, since the centres are not uniformly distributed along the network, but in the opposite direction to clustering. This is regularity (dispersion, inhibition). At longer distances the observed curve returns inside the envelope, so beyond that range the pattern is indistinguishable from random.
The seed is fixed above so these ranges are reproducible; without it the exact crossing distances shift on every rebuild.

title: Network Constrained Spatial Point Patterns Analysis
section: 8. What I Take From This Exercise
text:
8. What I Take From This Exercise
The result contradicts Exercise 2, and the contradiction is the whole lesson. Exercise 2 Part 02 concluded that childcare centres cluster at short range. Measured along the road network, the same kind of test on Punggol says the opposite: over the mid-range distances in the table above, centres are further apart than chance.
I do not think either result is wrong. They are answering different questions:

The planar K-function asks “are centres closer together than random points scattered over this polygon?” A large share of that polygon is water, park and reserve where nothing can be built, so the random comparison points are spread over space that real centres can never occupy. Against that null, anything confined to buildable land looks clustered.
The network K-function asks “are centres closer together than random points scattered over this road network?” That null already excludes the unbuildable space. What is left is the actual siting decision, and that decision turns out to space centres out, roughly one per residential precinct, which is exactly what a planner allocating childcare places by catchment would do.

So the planar “clustering” in Exercise 2 was substantially an artefact of the null, not a finding about childcare policy. That is an uncomfortable thing to discover about work I had already written up, and it is the strongest argument I have seen for why the network-constrained method exists.
Where the method is fragile. Three things would change the answer and none of them are statistical:

Bandwidth. 300m is a defensible walking distance, but it is a choice, and the hotspots move if I halve or double it. There is no bw.diggle equivalent here that picks it for me.
Network completeness. Punggol_St is a road network. Parents in Punggol walk through void decks, park connectors and the waterway bridges, none of which are in this layer. The network I am measuring distance on is not the network people use.
method = "simple". It duplicates kernel mass at intersections, and Punggol is full of intersections. The continuous method exists precisely to fix this and I would want to re-run with it before quoting any of these density values as real.

On nsim = 50. The chapter uses 50 simulations and I have kept that, but 50 is thin for a 95% envelope. It puts the pointwise significance level at 2/51, close enough to 0.04 that a marginal result would not survive scrutiny. Here the observed curve sits clearly outside the envelope across a contiguous band of distances rather than grazing it at a single point, so the conclusion holds. A single-band excursion would have been a reason to raise nsim rather than report it.
Connecting back. Reading Exercise 2 and this one together is the actual lesson. First-order KDE says where events are dense. Second-order G/F/K/L say whether events interact. Network-constrained versions say whether either conclusion survives once you stop pretending people travel in straight lines and stop pretending reservoirs are candidate sites. Each layer removed an assumption the previous one was quietly making, and unlike the first two steps, this one did not confirm the earlier answer. It reversed it. The thing I will carry forward is that in spatial statistics the null hypothesis is a modelling choice as consequential as the estimator, and a result is only as meaningful as the randomness it was compared against.

section: 6. Clark-Evans Test for Nearest Neighbour Analysis
text:
6. Clark-Evans Test for Nearest Neighbour Analysis
The Clark-Evans R statistic is the ratio of observed mean nearest-neighbour distance to the distance expected under complete spatial randomness (CSR).

R = 1 → random
R < 1 → clustered
R > 1 → regular / dispersed

\(H_0\): the distribution of childcare centres is randomly distributed. \(H_1\): the distribution is not randomly distributed. Confidence level 95%, so I reject \(H_0\) if p < 0.05.

6.1 Without CSR Simulation

clarkevans.test(childcareSG_ppp,
                correction = "none",
                clipregion = "sg_owin",
                alternative = c("clustered"),
                nsim = 99)


    Clark-Evans test
    No edge correction
    Z-test

data:  childcareSG_ppp
R = 0.50996, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: clustered (R < 1)




6.2 With CSR Simulation
On the number of simulations. The reference chapter uses nsim = 999. Each simulation has to scatter 1,925 random points inside Singapore’s full multipolygon boundary, which is slow enough at 999 that it dominates the build time for this whole site. I use nsim = 99, which gives a pointwise two-sided level of 2/100 = 0.02, still well inside the 0.05 I am testing at. The observed R sits far outside the simulated range rather than near its edge, so the conclusion does not depend on the extra simulations.

clarkevans.test(childcareSG_ppp,
                correction = "none",
                clipregion = NULL,
                alternative = c("clustered"),
                method = "MonteCarlo",
                nsim = 99)


    Clark-Evans test
    No edge correction
    Monte Carlo test based on 99 simulations of CSR with fixed n

data:  childcareSG_ppp
R = 0.50996, p-value = 0.01
alternative hypothesis: clustered (R < 1)








ImportantConclusion of the test



R is well below 1 and p is far below 0.05 under both the analytical Z-test and the Monte Carlo version, so I reject the null hypothesis. Childcare centres in Singapore are clustered, not randomly distributed. The Monte Carlo version is the one I would quote, because it does not depend on the asymptotic normality assumption that the plain Z-test makes.

NoteWhich bandwidth I would use



bw.CvL returns a much larger bandwidth and produces a smooth blob that says little beyond “the middle and east are busier”. bw.diggle and bw.ppl are far tighter and resolve individual towns. Baddeley’s advice is that bw.ppl is preferable when the pattern is a collection of tight clusters, and bw.diggle when the goal is detecting a single dominant cluster. Childcare centres are clearly the former, being many town-sized clusters, so bw.ppl is the more defensible choice here, even though the chapter demonstrates bw.diggle first.

8. Fixed and Adaptive Bandwidth KDE

8.1 Fixed Bandwidth
A fixed 600m bandwidth (0.6 in km units):

                               edge = TRUE,

plot(kde_childcareSG_600, main = "Fixed bandwidth, sigma = 600m")










8.2 Adaptive Bandwidth
Fixed bandwidth is a problem when the underlying point density varies a lot across the study area, which is exactly the case in Singapore, where the centre is dense and the west is sparse. Adaptive bandwidth varies the smoothing locally.

kde_childcareSG_adaptive <- adaptive.density(childcareSG_ppp.km, method = "kernel")
plot(kde_childcareSG_adaptive, main = "Adaptive bandwidth KDE")

plot(kde_childcareSG.bw, main = "Fixed bandwidth")
plot(kde_childcareSG_adaptive, main = "Adaptive bandwidth")







par(mfrow = c(1, 1))







NoteFixed vs adaptive



The adaptive surface keeps detail in the sparse western and northern areas that the fixed-bandwidth version smooths into near-nothing, while holding the dense central corridor together instead of fragmenting it. The trade-off is that the adaptive map is harder to explain to a non-technical reader, because the amount of smoothing is no longer constant across the map, so two equally bright pixels do not necessarily mean the same thing.

title: First-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis
section: 11. What I Take From This Exercise
text:
11. What I Take From This Exercise
The statistical answer. Childcare centres in Singapore are clustered at the national scale, decisively so, at R = 0.51 with p effectively zero under Monte Carlo simulation. The high-density areas are the mature and newer HDB towns.
The methodological point that cost me the most time. The window matters as much as the points. Running Clark-Evans on the national pattern and running it on Choa Chu Kang are answering different questions, and the second is not a “zoomed-in” version of the first. Changing the window changes the expected nearest-neighbour distance under CSR, which is the denominator of R. A pattern can be clustered nationally and close to random within a single town, and that is not a contradiction.
What I would flag as a limitation. The whole analysis treats Singapore’s land area as uniformly available for childcare centres, which is plainly false. Catchment reserves, airbases, port land and industrial estates cannot host a childcare centre at all. A clustering result measured against a CSR null that allows points anywhere on land will therefore always look clustered, partly for reasons that have nothing to do with childcare policy. A more honest null would restrict the window to residential-zoned land. That is beyond this exercise, but it is the first thing I would change.
Connecting to Part 02. First-order analysis stops at “where is it dense”. It cannot distinguish a pattern that is dense because the population is dense from a pattern that is dense because centres genuinely attract each other. The G, F, K and L functions in Part 02 are what separate those two.

title: Where peat burns, and how close together
text:
1.1 The problem the data creates
One thing has to be said before any analysis, because it governs every interpretation that follows.
A VIIRS active-fire detection is not a fire. It is a 375 m pixel in which a radiometer measured a thermal anomaly during a single overpass. A large peat fire covering ten square kilometres produces many dozens of detections in one pass. Two satellites pass overhead roughly four times a day between them, so the same fire is detected repeatedly. A detection therefore records sensor sampling of fire, not fire occurrence, and any statistic computed on the raw detection set partly measures the instrument.
The consequence is that the textbook second-order question, “is this pattern clustered relative to complete spatial randomness”, has a known answer before any computation. It is clustered, overwhelmingly, and would be clustered even if fires were sited completely at random, because each fire generates a burst of spatially adjacent detections. Reporting that rejection as a finding would be close to meaningless.
Section 6 therefore does two things instead: it changes the unit of analysis from the detection to the 375 m cell, and it changes the null model from complete spatial randomness to an inhomogeneous Poisson process. Both are stated here, at the front, because they are the substantive methodological content of the exercise rather than technical housekeeping.

Pulang Pisau wins that rule outright, at 3656 detections per 1,000 km². Two alternatives were seriously considered and rejected, and the reasons are recorded because a choice is only reviewable alongside them.
Ketapang leads on absolute count, with 65,901 detections against Pulang Pisau’s 35,679. It was not chosen because it covers 29,722 km², slightly over three times the area, and ranks second on density. Its larger count is mostly a larger window.
Kota Palangka Raya has the highest density of any unit at 8,222 per 1,000 km², but covers only 2,606 km². A 5 km lag there is a substantial fraction of the window’s own width, so edge effects would govern the second-order results.
Pulang Pisau is also rank 2 of 56 on raw count, so the rule does not select an obscure unit. Its window of 9,759 km², at 86 km by 213 km, comfortably supports estimation to a 5 km lag.
An earlier iteration of this analysis selected the regency on a seven-day sample of the same feed, on which Pulang Pisau led on count. Over the full window it does not. The selection rule above was therefore restated against the complete record, and it is reported here rather than quietly corrected, because a rule chosen after seeing which unit it favours is not a rule.

title: Where peat burns, and how close together
text:
3.3 Point event definition
I define an event as one 375 m grid cell in which at least one qualifying VIIRS detection was recorded. Qualifying means all of the following, and I have given the reason for each rather than just the rule.

Sensor and product
VIIRS 375 m I-band, Collection 2, S-NPP or NOAA-20. MODIS is excluded: its
1 km footprint is coarser than the distances this analysis is about, so including
it would blur the very scale under study.
Confidence
Nominal or high. Low-confidence detections are dropped. They are dominated by
small or cool anomalies and by edge-of-scan geometry, so retaining them would
make apparent intensity vary with viewing angle rather than with fire.
Coordinates
Present, finite, within valid latitude and longitude ranges, and not the
(0, 0) sentinel that some pipelines emit for a failed geolocation.
Timestamp
A parseable UTC acquisition time. Converted to WITA (UTC+8), because the
definition of a fire day and any reading of diurnal behaviour must be local.
Location
Strictly within the Pulang Pisau polygon. This also serves as the offshore
screen, since the polygon is terrestrial.
Not a fixed installation
See the persistence screen below. This substitutes for a field the NRT
product does not carry.
Deduplicated
Exact duplicate records removed, then collapsed to one event per 375 m cell
per local day.

I build three patterns from the same screened detections, because which unit is right depends on which question I am asking:








Pattern
Unit
Used for




ppp_all
every retained detection
sensitivity checks only


ppp_daycell
one event per 375 m cell per local day
spatio-temporal analysis


ppp_cell
one event per 375 m cell over the window
primary spatial analysis



I use ppp_cell as the primary spatial pattern because it removes the repeat-detection inflation I described in Section 1.1. A cell that burned for three weeks and was detected eighty times contributes one point, not eighty.
For the representative point of each cell I take the earliest detection in it. That is deterministic and it keeps a real sensor coordinate. I considered snapping to cell centres and rejected it, because that would impose a regular lattice and manufacture apparent regularity at small lags, which would contaminate exactly the statistic the rest of the report depends on.

title: Where peat burns, and how close together
text:
3.4 Spatial study window
My window is the Pulang Pisau administrative polygon, unbuffered, in WGS 84 / UTM zone 49S (EPSG:32749).
Projecting is not optional here. Every second-order statistic I use is a function of Euclidean distance in metres, and at this latitude one degree of longitude is about 111 km while one degree of latitude is about 110.6 km. If I worked in degrees I would be building a systematic anisotropy into every distance I compute. Zone 49S is the right one for a regency centroid at 113.96°E, which sits inside the zone’s 108°E to 114°E span. I checked the eastern edge, which reaches 114.35°E and is marginally outside, and the resulting scale error is below 0.1%, so it does not matter at the kilometre scales I work at.
I used the administrative boundary rather than a buffered or natural window because the management question is administrative: a regency fire agency has jurisdiction to that line. The cost is a real edge effect, since fires obviously do not stop at a boundary, and I handle it with edge correction rather than pretending it is not there (Section 5).

Table 3: Retention probe. Single-day FIRMS NRT queries over a Kalimantan-wide box. Exactly zero detections across a 10.6<U+00B0> by 9.7<U+00B0> box for every sampled date from January to 30 June is not a physically credible result for Borneo, so the zeros are read as absence of coverage. The standard-processing archive, queried for the same region in August, also returns zero rows: it has not yet been built for 2026.




The FIRMS area REST endpoint serves near-real-time granules on a rolling retention of roughly 90 days, and the standard-processing product has not been produced for 2026 yet, because NRT granules are only replaced by standard science quality data after a lag of about five months. So the earliest day the API will give me is 1 July 2026, which I located to the day with the probe above rather than assuming it. The upper bound is my choice: the last complete UTC day before I accessed the data, so that no partially observed day enters the daily series and shows up as a fake decline.
I should be precise about what that constraint is and is not, because it would be easy to overstate it. The 90-day limit belongs to the API, not to the data. FIRMS also publishes an archive download service covering VIIRS S-NPP from 20 January 2012 and NOAA-20 from 1 April 2018. It is a request form rather than a REST endpoint: it authenticates through an Earthdata login or an emailed verification code, and it delivers the extract by email afterwards. That is a perfectly obtainable dataset, and the reason this report does not use it is a scripting constraint rather than a data constraint. My pipeline is built to run unattended from a single key, and the archive service cannot be driven that way.
The honest statement is therefore that I chose a 87-day window served by the API over a multi-year window that would have required an out-of-band request. Section 12 records what that cost me.
I want to be careful not to oversell the window. It is what was available. But it does happen to span the onset, escalation and peak of the 2026 dry season, which is the period a fire agency actually acts over. If the retention limit had cut off the peak instead of the wet-season baseline I would have had to change the study design entirely. The honest cost is that I cannot make any wet-season comparison, so nothing in this report speaks to the seasonal amplitude of fire activity, only to its structure within one season. I repeat that in Section 12 because it is a real limit on what I can claim.

Counting downloaded rows does not establish that the record is complete. The specific failure that matters for a daily series is a request that returns empty: it is indistinguishable from a day on which nothing burned, and it would appear in the analysis as a decline in fire activity.
The audit is therefore constructed to catch that. Each of the two platforms should contribute at least one detection somewhere in Kalimantan on every day of an 87-day dry season, because an island-sized box is never entirely without fire. Any day on which a platform contributes nothing is a candidate failure.

4.2 The missing type field, and what replaces it
The FIRMS standard-processing product carries a type field distinguishing vegetation fire (0) from active volcano (1), other static land source (2) and offshore (3). The NRT product used here does not carry it, verified against the API response header: column present = FALSE. The screen it would have provided has to be reconstructed.

Volcanoes (type 1) pose no risk. Borneo has no Holocene volcano. The screen is unnecessary rather than approximated.
Offshore (type 3) is removed by the clip to the terrestrial polygon.
Other static land sources (type 2) are a genuine contamination risk. Kalimantan has palm-oil mills, coal operations and gas flares, all of which present as persistent thermal anomalies. This is the case that needs work.

The substitute is a persistence screen. A vegetation fire burns out or moves; a flare stack does not. Each 375 m cell is scored by the number of distinct local dates on which it was detected, as a fraction of the 87-day window, and cells above a threshold are removed as fixed installations.

text:
4.4 Geometry validation
I checked the boundary polygon for validity before using it. It is a single valid polygon, so I did not need any multipart or self-intersection handling, though I ran st_make_valid anyway as a defensive step. For point-in-polygon assignment I used st_within rather than st_intersects, so a detection sitting exactly on the boundary arc is excluded rather than double-counted against a neighbouring regency. spatstat’s window conversion reported no points rejected as outside the window, which tells me my clip and the owin agree.
Two things here commonly go wrong and I handled them deliberately. First, I assigned regencies to parent provinces by testing containment of an interior representative point in a projected coordinate system, not by nearest-feature matching. Nearest feature would silently mis-assign any regency whose representative point fell marginally outside its own province, and I would never have noticed. Second, I read the 159 MB national ADM2 file through a bounding-box filter at the GDAL level rather than loading it and subsetting afterwards, so the full national geometry is never held in memory.

Two of these deserve a note.
Border versus Ripley correction. Ripley’s isotropic correction is more efficient but costs substantially more computation, and the envelope procedure requires 199 re-computations. Table 12: Bandwidth selectors compared on the primary pattern, ordered as computed. The spread is a factor of roughly eighteen from smallest to largest, which is why reporting a single surface without this table would conceal the most consequential choice in the first-order analysis.




The two cross-validation selectors return sub-kilometre bandwidths, 573 m for bw.ppl and 628 m for bw.diggle, and density.ppp emits a numerical-underflow warning at that scale over a window of 9,759 km². Neither was adopted, and the reason is not that the warning is inconvenient.
Cross-validation selectors are documented to choose very small bandwidths when a pattern is strongly clustered at short range. Their criteria reward a surface that reproduces the local bursts, so they interpret clustering as fine-grained intensity structure. That is a reasonable thing to want in some applications, and the wrong thing to want here, because the same estimate is used as the reference intensity for the second-order test in Section 7.3. If \(\hat{\lambda}(u)\) has already absorbed the sub-kilometre clustering, then asking whether clustering remains after removing \(\hat{\lambda}(u)\) is a rigged question, and the answer would be no by construction.
The adopted bandwidth is therefore fixed at 4,000 m, on a criterion stated before the surfaces were inspected: it must exceed the interaction range, so that trend and interaction are estimated by separate parts of the analysis rather than competing for the same signal. Four kilometres sits above the roughly 2 km interaction range that Section 7.3 goes on to find, inside the interval spanned by the two components of bw.scott (3,847 m and 10,543 m), and below bw.CvL (10,530 m).
This is a judgement, not an optimisation, and it is stated as one. The comparison below shows what each alternative would have produced, so a reader who disagrees can see the consequence rather than having to take the choice on trust.


code
bw_panels <- list(
  ppl   = glue("bw.ppl, {round(FO$sigma_ppl)} m (rejected)"),
  main  = glue("adopted, {fmt_n(FO$sigma_main)} m"),
  scott = glue("bw.scott x, {fmt_n(round(FO$sigma_scott[1]))} m"),
  CvL   = glue("bw.CvL, {fmt_n(round(FO$sigma_CvL))} m"))
bw_df <- bind_rows(lapply(names(bw_panels), function(k)
  im_df(FO$kde[[k]]) |> mutate(panel = bw_panels[[k]]))) |>
  mutate(v = per_1000km2(intensity))
bw_df$panel <- factor(bw_df$panel, levels = unlist(bw_panels))
ggplot(bw_df) +
  geom_raster(aes(x, y, fill = v)) +
  geom_sf(data = win_p, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_intensity(v = bw_df$v) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA, expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "What the bandwidth decides") +
  theme_map(base_size = 9)








Figure 4: The same pattern under four bandwidths. Reading: the choice is not cosmetic. The cross-validated surface resolves individual fire complexes and, at this sample size, a great deal of structure no agency could act on; it is also the surface that would sabotage the second-order test, for the reason given above. The 10.5 km bw.CvL surface is stable but has smoothed away the distinction between the peat belt and its margins, which is the distinction of interest. The adopted 4 km surface and bw.scott’s 3.8 km are visually close, which is reassurance that the adopted value is not an idiosyncratic pick. The important disclosure is that all four agree on the location of the principal concentration and disagree on how many secondary concentrations exist, so no claim about secondary hotspots is made.

Figure 5: Estimated first-order intensity of burned cells, Gaussian kernel with Diggle’s edge correction, at the adopted 4 km bandwidth. Reading: intensity is organised as a broad south-southeast band reaching a maximum in the lower third of the regency, with a secondary extension along the eastern margin. The empty northern interior is a real absence rather than an absence of observation: the same satellites observed it on the same days. The gradient is steep, spanning roughly two orders of magnitude between the peat belt and the northern interior, which means resource allocation proportional to intensity would be very unevenly distributed. That is the operational content of a first-order surface, and it is the strongest planning-relevant result the first-order analysis alone supports.





An adaptive estimator was computed as a check, since a fixed bandwidth over-smooths sparse areas and under-smooths dense ones. It reproduces the same principal concentration, which is the reassurance sought: the reported structure is not an artefact of assuming one bandwidth everywhere.

6.6 Radiative power, not just counts
A count surface treats a barely detectable smouldering pixel and an intense flaming front as the same event, which bothered me. Fire radiative power is the sensor’s estimate of radiative output in megawatts, so smoothing that instead answers a different and arguably more useful question.

frpt_df <- im_df(FO$frp_total, "v") |> mutate(v = v * 1e6, panel = "Total FRP released (MW per km²)")

  geom_sf(data = win_p, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = PAL$seq, name = "MW") +
  coord_sf(datum = NA, expand = FALSE) + labs(subtitle = "Mean FRP per detection") + theme_map(9)
p2 <- ggplot(frpt_df) + geom_raster(aes(x, y, fill = v)) +
  geom_sf(data = win_p, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = PAL$seq, trans = "sqrt", name = "MW/km\u00b2",
                       labels = label_number(big.mark = ",")) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA, expand = FALSE) + labs(subtitle = "Total FRP released") + theme_map(9)

                          theme = theme_ex01())








Figure 6: Left, mean fire radiative power per detection. Right, total radiative power released, which is intensity and mean power combined. What I take from it: the two panels separate two things a single count map conflates. Total power (right) closely tracks detection intensity, so the southern peat belt dominates energy release as well as event count. Mean power per detection (left) has a different geography: it is comparatively low across the core of the peat belt and higher on the margins and in the sparse north. That is consistent with the physical expectation that peat combustion is low-intensity and persistent while fires on mineral soil and in cleared vegetation burn hotter and shorter. It is also a caution to me: the places with the most detections are not the places with the most intense individual fires.

Reading: every statistic departs from the CSR envelope immediately and by an enormous margin. G rises far faster than expected, meaning nearest neighbours are much closer than random; F rises far slower, meaning empty gaps are much larger than random; L sits far above zero at every lag. Read naively this is overwhelming evidence of clustering. Read correctly it is evidence of almost nothing, because the sensor guarantees this result: a single fire produces adjacent detections. 7.2 What the pair correlation function reveals about the instrument
\(K\) and \(L\) are cumulative, which means a departure at one lag propagates into every larger lag and I cannot see where anything is actually happening. The pair correlation function \(g(r)\) is a density rather than a cumulative quantity, so it separates scales properly. This turned out to matter more than I expected.


code
pcf_df <- SO$pcf_obs |> filter(is.finite(trans), r > 0)
ggplot(pcf_df, aes(r, trans)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = DEDUP_GRID_M, colour = PAL$cool, linetype = "12", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
  annotate("text", x = DEDUP_GRID_M + 60, y = max(pcf_df$trans) * 0.85,
           label = "375 m pixel", hjust = 0, size = 2.9, colour = PAL$cool,
           family = "Helvetica") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "r", y = "g(r), log scale",
       title = "The sensor's footprint is visible in the statistic",
       subtitle = "Suppression below one pixel width is an instrument property, not fire behaviour.") +
  theme_ex01()








Figure 10: Pair correlation function of the primary pattern, log scale. The dotted line marks the 375 m VIIRS pixel dimension. What I take from it: g(r) is suppressed at very short range and peaks at about 460 m, immediately above the pixel width. This is not fires avoiding one another. It is the sensor’s resolution: two detections cannot be much closer than one pixel, because one pixel yields one detection. That short-range suppression is an instrument artefact and is the clearest single piece of evidence that this pattern records observation rather than events. Above the peak, g(r) decays slowly and is still above 3 at 2.9 km, nowhere near its asymptote of 1. So spatial dependence extends well beyond the 5 km range I plot here, which is what pushed me to Section 7.5.

text:
7.3 The test that can fail
These are the statistics I actually trust. My null is an inhomogeneous Poisson process whose intensity is the kernel estimate from Section 6.5, so everything my first-order analysis established is already inside the null. If I get a departure now, it means residual interaction rather than large-scale variation, which is the question I set in Q3.


code
# An envelope built from `simulate=` has no theoretical curve, only the simulation
# mean, so the reference is set explicitly: 0 for the centred L function and 1 for
# the pair correlation function.
li <- SO$env_Linhom |> mutate(across(c(obs, lo, hi), ~ .x - r),
                              ref = 0, panel = "L_inhom(r) - r")
gi <- SO$env_pcfinhom |> filter(r > 0) |> mutate(ref = 1, panel = "g_inhom(r)")
ggplot(bind_rows(li, gi), aes(r)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_line(aes(y = ref), colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(aes(y = obs), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  labs(x = "r", y = NULL,
       title = "Clustering survives the honest null, and has a scale",
       subtitle = glue("Envelope from {SO$nsim} simulations of an inhomogeneous Poisson process with lambda re-estimated each time.")) +
  theme_ex01(base_size = 9)








Figure 11: Inhomogeneous centred L function and inhomogeneous pair correlation function, against envelopes from 199 simulations of an inhomogeneous Poisson process. The reference intensity is re-estimated for every simulated pattern. What I take from it: the departure survives, and it does not close. Both curves leave the envelope at about 100 m and remain outside it across the entire range plotted. g_inhom peaks near 5.9 at roughly 570 m and is still above 2 at 2.8 km, against an envelope ceiling near 1.4. So after accounting for the fact that fire is far more likely in the southern peat belt than in the north, burned cells still occur much closer together than that variation alone predicts. Note also that g_inhom falls below 1 at the shortest lags, the sensor floor surviving into the inhomogeneous statistic.

Both global tests reject the inhomogeneous Poisson null at the Monte Carlo floor. So the pattern is clustered beyond its first-order trend, which is the answer to the first half of Q3.
What I could not establish from this was where the clustering ends, and that is down to a decision of mine that turned out to be wrong. I capped the r range at 5 km, reasoning that longer lags in an elongated window rest on too few pairs. But across the whole of that range both curves sit outside the envelope, which means 5 km only establishes that dependence extends at least that far. My cap was too conservative to answer the question I had set it to answer. Section 7.5 is where I fix it.
The direction of the remaining bias matters for how confidently this can be stated. As set out in assumption A6, estimating \(\hat{\lambda}\) from the pattern under test lets it absorb part of the clustering, which widens the envelope and makes the test harder to reject. The rejection therefore stands despite a conservative procedure, not because of a permissive one.

  SO$Linhom_cell |> transmute(r, v = border - r, pattern = "ppp_cell (reported)"),
  SO$Linhom_all  |> transmute(r, v = border - r, pattern = "ppp_all (un-thinned)"))

  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +

Figure 13: Inhomogeneous centred L function computed on the cell pattern and on the un-thinned detection pattern, on a common axis. What I take from it: both curves are positive, so the qualitative conclusion of residual clustering does not depend on the event definition. The magnitudes differ by roughly an order of magnitude, and the un-thinned pattern shows far stronger apparent clustering at every lag. That gap is the repeat-detection artefact measured directly. It is why I use the cell pattern for inference and the detection pattern only for this check. If I reported the upper curve I would be reporting the satellite revisit schedule as a fire-behaviour result.

section: 7.5 Extending the range, and what it costs to have been wrong
text:
7.5 Extending the range, and what it costs to have been wrong
The 5 km cap was set on the reasoning that long lags in an elongated window rest on few pairs. That reasoning is sound, but 5 km was more conservative than necessary: the rule stated in Section 5 caps \(r\) at a quarter of the window’s shortest dimension, and the window is 86 km wide, so 20 km was admissible all along. Extending to 20 km is not a post-hoc licence, it is applying the rule that was already stated.
Two practical constraints follow, and both are disclosed rather than absorbed. pcfinhom offers no border correction, and the translation correction over roughly seven million pairs per pattern did not complete in a workable time for 99 simulated patterns. So significance across the extended range rests on \(L_{inhom}\) with a border correction and a full envelope, while the shape of \(g_{inhom}\) across that range comes from a single translation-corrected curve with no simulations. No significance claim is made for \(g_{inhom}\) beyond 3 km.

  transmute(r, obs = trans, lo = NA_real_, hi = NA_real_, ref = 1,
            panel = "g_inhom(r), observed only")

  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.75, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_line(aes(y = ref), colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(aes(y = obs), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +

section: 9.1 What is the clustering organised around?
text:
9.1 What is the clustering organised around?
Peat fire in this landscape is overwhelmingly human in ignition and made possible by drainage. I picked two mapped covariates to proxy those mechanisms: distance to the road network, for access and ignition opportunity, and distance to mapped canals and waterways, for drainage-driven desiccation.
I took the covariate geometry from a dated Geofabrik OpenStreetMap extract for Kalimantan rather than a live Overpass query. That was not my first choice. Overpass refused a bounding box this size repeatedly, and once I had switched I realised the extract is better anyway: a live query returns different data every time it runs, so it cannot be part of a reproducible pipeline. The extract gave me 28,515 road features and 3,061 waterway features within a 15 km buffer of the regency.
I compute distances on that buffered frame and only then crop to the analysis window. If I had computed them on the clipped window I would have biased every distance upward for cells near the boundary, because their nearest road is often outside the regency entirely.
The 3,061 waterway features against 28,515 road features is itself my first result here, and it is a warning rather than a finding. An area defined by an abandoned canal network has fewer mapped watercourses than roads. I come back to what that does to the drainage covariate below.

  d <- rh
  nm <- names(d)

         lo = if ("lo" %in% nm) d[["lo"]] else NA_real_,

title: Where peat burns, and how close together
text:
9.2 How large is a cluster?
A significance test tells me clustering exists. A fitted cluster process tells me how big it is, which is the form a planner could actually use. Getting that number right meant throwing away my first answer.
I first fitted a Thomas process with no trend term. It returned a cluster standard deviation of 3,292 m, about 440 events per cluster, and an implied 24 parent locations in the entire regency. Twenty-three clusters of 440 events each across a whole regency did not sound like a cluster scale to me, and it is not. It is the southern peat belt being re-described as a handful of enormous clusters, which is the only way a model with no trend term can represent large-scale intensity variation. This is the standard identifiability problem between trend and interaction in cluster processes. If I had taken the number at face value I would have reported a confident and completely wrong operational radius.
The fix is to remove the trend before estimating the cluster parameters. My inhomogeneous pair correlation function already does exactly that, because it divides out \(\hat{\lambda}(u)\). So I fitted the Thomas pair correlation function
\[g(r) \;=\; 1 + \frac{1}{4\pi\kappa\sigma^{2}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{r^{2}}{4\sigma^{2}}\right)\]
directly to \(g_{inhom}\) by minimum contrast, minimising \(\sum_r \left(\hat{g}(r)^{q} - g_\theta(r)^{q}\right)^{2}\) with \(q = 1/4\) over \(r \in [200, 5,000]\) m. I set the lower limit to exclude lags governed by the 375 m sensor floor rather than by the cluster process. I wrote the fit out explicitly in R/07_cluster_scale.R rather than calling a packaged routine, because the objective function and the excluded range are the substance of the estimate and I wanted them visible.

The shaded band marks lags below 200 m, excluded from the fit because they are governed by the sensor’s pixel size. What I take from it: the trend-removed fit tracks the observed curve closely from the peak outward, which is the range that matters for an operational radius. The fit that retains the trend is too flat and too wide, because its cluster component is doing work that belongs to the intensity surface. Neither fit captures the observed curve beyond about 4 km, where the observed g_inhom decays more slowly than a single Gaussian cluster kernel allows. That is a real limitation of my model: the pattern has structure at more than one scale, and a one-scale model cannot represent it.





My trend-removed fit gives a cluster standard deviation of 1,055 m, so about 95% of the events in a cluster fall within roughly 2,581 m of its centre, with 67 events per cluster and about 155 cluster centres across the regency. That is consistent with my pair correlation function, which peaks at 438 m, and I got there by a different route: minimum contrast fitting of a mechanistic model rather than envelope testing.
Two estimates agreeing is stronger than either alone, but the agreement is only partial and I should say where it breaks. My fitted model has a single scale, and the figure below shows the observed curve decaying more slowly beyond about 4 km than a single Gaussian kernel allows. So the Thomas process describes the dominant local structure well and the longer tail of dependence out to roughly 7.2 km not at all. A multi-scale cluster process, or a log-Gaussian Cox process with a flexible covariance, would be the natural next model. Fitting one is beyond what I can do in this exercise, but it is the first thing I would try next.
