title: Where peat burns, and how close together
text:
11.1 Consistency across approaches
My first-order and second-order analyses agree where they should and disagree in two places, and the disagreements taught me more than the agreement did.
They agree on the dominant scale. My inhomogeneous pair correlation function peaks at 438 m. My Thomas process fitted to that same curve returns a cluster standard deviation of 1,055 m. Two estimates from different machinery, one envelope-based and one model-based, both put the dominant structure at roughly a kilometre. That agreement is the main reason I am willing to quote a number.
They disagree about extent, and it is the cumulative statistic that misled me. \(L_{inhom}\) never re-enters its envelope within 20 km, which tempted me to conclude that dependence extends at least that far. \(g_{inhom}\), which localises scale instead of accumulating it, shows the excess is within 10% of nothing by about 7.2 km. Both computations are correct and the second is the one I report, because \(L\) accumulates every excess at smaller lags and therefore stays elevated long past the range over which anything is actually happening. This is a general property of \(K\) and \(L\) rather than a quirk of my data, and it is probably the single most useful thing I learned doing this exercise.
They disagree about sufficiency, and my first-order surface loses. My earlier version, capped at a 5 km lag, concluded that the intensity surface was an adequate description above about 2 km. That was wrong, and wrong because of a decision rather than a computation: my cap was too short to see where dependence ended. Corrected, the first-order surface is not a sufficient description at any lag below roughly 7.2 km. A smooth intensity map is still a reasonable tool for allocating resources across a regency. It is not a tool for anticipating what happens next around a fire that has already started.
My covariate models sharpen this rather than softening it. They improve on an intercept-only model by 2,005 AIC units, so a lot of the first-order variation is explained by accessibility. But the residual \(K\) function shows they capture none of the local interaction. Location explains where fire is likely. It does not explain the contagion.

title: Where peat burns, and how close together
text:
10.2 Where the analysis is weakest
Three places, in order of severity.
The event definition does the heavy lifting. Collapsing detections to cells is defensible and necessary, but it is a modelling decision presented as data preparation. A cell that burned for three weeks and a cell that burned for one overpass contribute identically to ppp_cell. An analysis weighting cells by persistence or by cumulative radiative power would answer a related but different question and might not reach the same conclusion about scale.
The inhomogeneous null is estimated from the data under test. The bias is in the conservative direction, so the rejection stands, but the magnitude of the excess clustering is not reliably estimated. Statements about how much clustering there is should be read as ordinal, not quantitative.
Detectability is confounded with intensity. Assumptions A1 and A2 cannot be discharged within this data source. Sub-surface peat smouldering, the mode of greatest public-health concern, is systematically under-detected, and cloud cover is not plausibly independent of location. The intensity surface is a surface of detected fire.
One analytical decision was simply wrong and had to be reversed. The r range was initially capped at 5 km. Every inhomogeneous statistic sat outside its envelope across the whole of that range, which means the cap could not answer the question it was set to answer, and the first draft of this report drew a conclusion from it that the extended analysis contradicts. The cap is recorded here rather than silently replaced, because a range chosen before seeing the curves and then revised when the curves demanded it is a different thing from a range chosen to produce a tidy answer, and a reader has no way to tell the two apart unless told.

title: Where peat burns, and how close together
text:
Contents

One argument running through all of it: a satellite hotspot is not a fire, and almost everything I did follows from taking that seriously.

text:
3. A detection is not a fire













One large peat fire fills many 375 m pixels, and two satellites re-detect it about four times a day.
I measured it: the raw count overstates distinct burning locations by 3.4x.
So the pattern I started with partly measures the satellite’s revisit schedule, which means testing against complete spatial randomness was guaranteed to reject before I computed anything.
So I changed two things. The unit becomes the 375 m cell. The null becomes an inhomogeneous Poisson process.
That is the spine of everything else I did.

4. Where it burns













Gaussian kernel, Diggle edge correction, bandwidth I fixed at 4 km.
Cross-validated selectors gave me about 0.6 km and I rejected them: they absorb the very clustering my second-order test exists to detect, which would have rigged the test on Slide 7.
Intensity spans roughly two orders of magnitude between the southern peat belt and the northern interior.
So allocating in proportion to sub-district area is badly matched to risk. I think that is the most directly usable thing I found.

text:
6. Against CSR, everything is significant

Every statistic leaves the envelope immediately. This should persuade nobody, including me: the sensor guarantees it. I show it so the failure is visible rather than hidden.
My pair correlation function makes the point sharper. It is suppressed below 375 m, the pixel dimension. That apparent short-range inhibition is the instrument, not fires avoiding one another.

title: Where peat burns, and how close together
text:
7. The test that can fail













My null is an inhomogeneous Poisson process with intensity from the 4 km kernel estimate, so everything my first-order analysis found is already inside the null. I re-estimate the reference intensity for every simulated pattern.
The departure survives. Both global tests reject at the Monte Carlo floor.
The two panels disagree, and that was the lesson for me. L_inhom never re-enters its envelope in 20 km. g_inhom, which localises scale instead of accumulating it, peaks at 438 m and is within 10% of no-excess by 7.2 km.
L accumulates every excess at smaller lags, so it stays significant far past the range where anything is happening. My first draft capped r at 5 km and drew the wrong conclusion from exactly this.

title: Where peat burns, and how close together
section: 7. Space and time are not separable
text:
7. Space and time are not separable













Knox test. My null is random labelling: I hold locations and dates both fixed and permute only their pairing, across 999 permutations of 8,720,153 close pairs.
Because both marginals stay fixed, none of this can be explained away by the seasonal ramp or the spatial concentration.
Strongest at the tightest cell, decaying monotonically outward. I read that as short-range propagation: a cell that burns today raises the chance a neighbour burns tomorrow, and the effect is largely spent within days and a kilometre or two.
The decay is steeper in time than in space, which fits fire spreading over contiguous ground within days rather than recurring in the same place weeks apart.

section: 8. What it is organised around, and how big it is
text:
8. What it is organised around, and how big it is













Access dominates. Of 2,005 AIC units separating my covariate model from an intercept-only model, distance to road accounts for 1,991.
Mapped drainage adds almost nothing (13 AIC units). That is not evidence drainage does not matter: OSM does not map the Mega Rice Project canal network, so my covariate is measuring mapping coverage.
Cluster scale 1,055 m, 95% within 2,581 m, from a Thomas process I fitted to g_inhom by minimum contrast.
My first fit left the trend in and returned 3,292 m and 440 events per cluster, which is really the peat belt re-described as a few giant clusters. Trend and interaction are not separately identifiable unless I force them apart.
Residual K shows my covariates explain location, not contagion.

section: 10. What this supports, and what it does not
text:
10. What this supports, and what it does not


What I would act on
Reallocate by intensity, not by area. Two orders of magnitude separate the southern peat belt from the northern interior.
A containment geometry. First ring 2.6 km, elevation out to about 7.2 km, days not weeks. Two methods I ran independently agree on the dominant scale.
A monitoring limit. I cannot resolve anything below 375 m. A finer answer needs a different sensor, not a different statistic.


What I would not claim
Roads as a policy lever. Roads follow worked land. I cannot tell from this whether access aids suppression or enables ignition, and the two point opposite ways.
Any claim about drainage. My covariate measures OSM coverage.
Any claim about time of day. Four fixed overpasses.
That any of this describes a normal year. As the previous slide shows, 2026 is the second-worst season in fourteen years, so every scale here was measured under extreme conditions.



My technical report, code and audit trail are in the repository. Data: NASA FIRMS, geoBoundaries, OpenStreetMap via Geofabrik.

title: Where peat burns, and how close together
section: 1.1 The problem the data handed me
text:
1.1 The problem the data handed me
I need to state one thing before any analysis, because it ended up governing every interpretation I made.
A VIIRS active-fire detection is not a fire. It is a 375 m pixel in which a radiometer measured a thermal anomaly during a single overpass. A large peat fire covering ten square kilometres produces many dozens of detections in one pass, and the two satellites pass overhead roughly four times a day between them, so the same fire gets detected over and over. What a detection actually records is the sensor sampling fire, not fire occurrence. Any statistic I compute on the raw detection set is therefore partly measuring the instrument.
Once I realised that, the textbook second-order question stopped being interesting. “Is this pattern clustered relative to complete spatial randomness” already has a known answer before I compute anything. It is clustered, overwhelmingly, and it would still be clustered even if fires were sited completely at random, because each fire produces a burst of adjacent detections. Reporting that rejection as a finding would be close to meaningless, so I did not want to build the report on it.
Instead I changed two things, and I am stating them up front because they are the real methodological content of this exercise rather than housekeeping. I changed the unit of analysis from the detection to the 375 m cell, and I changed the null model from complete spatial randomness to an inhomogeneous Poisson process. Section 7 is where that pays off.

3.6 My completeness audit, and a real outage
Counting the rows I downloaded does not tell me the record is complete. The failure mode I was worried about is a request that comes back empty, because that is indistinguishable from a day on which nothing burned, and it would show up in my analysis as a drop in fire activity that never happened.
So I built the audit to catch exactly that. Each of the two platforms should contribute at least one detection somewhere in Kalimantan on every day of an 87-day dry season, because an island-sized box is never completely without fire. Any day where a platform contributes nothing is a candidate failure and worth chasing.

Six of the seven dates are consecutive, which made me suspect a real outage rather than a flaky connection. Re-querying confirmed it: Suomi NPP returns an empty result for 11 to 16 July and for 3 August no matter how many times I ask. So this is an absence in the FIRMS near-real-time record itself, not a transient request failure I could fix by retrying. On those seven days my analysis rests on NOAA-20 alone, and detection counts are depressed by roughly the contribution of one platform.
The consequence is small, but I do not want to write it off as nothing. Those dates carry 51 of 23,576 events, or 0.22% of the record, and all of them fall in the near-zero early season before the dry-season ramp. Mean daily events on the affected dates are 7.3 against 10.8 on nearby unaffected July dates, which is consistent with losing one platform on very small counts. No conclusion I draw turns on those seven days, but the reader should treat the early-season part of my daily series as a slight underestimate.

4.2 The missing type field, and what I replaced it with
This was the data-quality problem that took me longest to solve. The FIRMS standard-processing product carries a type field separating vegetation fire (0) from active volcano (1), other static land source (2) and offshore (3). The NRT product I have to use does not carry it, which I verified against the API response header rather than assuming: column present = FALSE. So I had to reconstruct the screen it would have given me.
I worked through the three cases separately:

Volcanoes (type 1) are not a risk at all. Borneo has no Holocene volcano, so this screen is unnecessary rather than approximated. I did not need to do anything.
Offshore (type 3) is already handled by my clip to the terrestrial polygon.
Other static land sources (type 2) are a genuine problem. Kalimantan has palm-oil mills, coal operations and gas flares, and all of them show up as persistent thermal anomalies. This is the case I actually had to solve.

My substitute is a persistence screen. The logic is that a vegetation fire burns out or moves, whereas a flare stack does not. So I score each 375 m cell by the number of distinct local dates on which it was detected, as a fraction of the 87-day window, and drop cells above a threshold as fixed installations.

Two of these are worth explaining properly.
Border versus Ripley correction. Ripley’s isotropic correction is more efficient but costs a lot more computation, and my envelope procedure needs 199 re-computations of it. At 10,321 points the efficiency I lose with the border correction does not matter, because the number of pairs contributing at each lag is already very large. So this is a compute trade-off and I made it deliberately rather than by accepting a default.
Global versus pointwise tests. This one took me a while to get straight. A pointwise envelope gets read at every one of several hundred values of \(r\), so the probability of at least one excursion under the null is far above the nominal level. I still plot the pointwise envelopes, because they show me where on the \(r\) axis the departure sits and a single p-value cannot. But every claim of significance I make in this report is backed by the MAD or DCLF global test, not by the band.

Table 12: Bandwidth selectors compared on the primary pattern, ordered as computed. The spread is a factor of roughly eighteen from smallest to largest, which is why reporting a single surface without this table would conceal the most consequential choice in the first-order analysis.




Both cross-validation selectors came back with sub-kilometre bandwidths, 573 m for bw.ppl and 628 m for bw.diggle, and density.ppp threw a numerical-underflow warning at that scale over a window of 9,759 km². I did not adopt either, and it is not because the warning was inconvenient.
Cross-validation selectors are documented to choose very small bandwidths when a pattern is strongly clustered at short range. Their criteria reward a surface that reproduces the local bursts, so they end up treating clustering as fine-grained intensity structure. In some applications that is exactly what you want. Here it is the opposite of what I want, because I use the same estimate as the reference intensity for the second-order test in Section 7.3. If \(\hat{\lambda}(u)\) has already soaked up the sub-kilometre clustering, then asking whether clustering remains after removing \(\hat{\lambda}(u)\) is a rigged question and the answer is no by construction. I would have produced a confident and meaningless result.
So I fixed the bandwidth at 4,000 m, on a criterion I set before looking at the surfaces: it has to exceed the interaction range, so that trend and interaction are estimated by separate parts of my analysis instead of competing for the same signal. Four kilometres sits above the interaction range Section 7 goes on to find, inside the interval spanned by the two components of bw.scott (3,847 m and 10,543 m), and below bw.CvL (10,530 m).
I want to be clear that this is a judgement and not an optimisation. The comparison below shows what each alternative would have given me, so anyone who disagrees can see the consequence rather than taking my word for it.

  CvL   = glue("bw.CvL, {fmt_n(round(FO$sigma_CvL))} m"))

  im_df(FO$kde[[k]]) |> mutate(panel = bw_panels[[k]]))) |>
  mutate(v = per_1000km2(intensity))
bw_df$panel <- factor(bw_df$panel, levels = unlist(bw_panels))
ggplot(bw_df) +
  geom_raster(aes(x, y, fill = v)) +
  geom_sf(data = win_p, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_intensity(v = bw_df$v) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA, expand = FALSE) +

  theme_map(base_size = 9)








Figure 4: The same pattern under four bandwidths. What I take from it: the choice is not cosmetic. The cross-validated surface resolves individual fire complexes and, at this sample size, a great deal of structure no agency could act on; it is also the surface that would sabotage the second-order test, for the reason given above. The 10.5 km bw.CvL surface is stable but has smoothed away the distinction between the peat belt and its margins, which is the distinction of interest. The adopted 4 km surface and bw.scott’s 3.8 km are visually close, which is reassurance that the adopted value is not an idiosyncratic pick. What I should disclose is that all four agree on where the principal concentration is and disagree on how many secondary ones exist, so I make no claim about secondary hotspots.

6.5 The intensity surface I report

       subtitle = glue("Kernel intensity estimate, sigma = {fmt_n(FO$sigma_main)} m, Diggle edge correction")) +
  theme_map() + theme(legend.position = "right", legend.key.height = unit(34, "pt"),
                      legend.key.width = unit(9, "pt"))








Figure 5: Estimated first-order intensity of burned cells, Gaussian kernel with Diggle’s edge correction, at the adopted 4 km bandwidth. What I take from it: intensity is organised as a broad south-southeast band reaching a maximum in the lower third of the regency, with a secondary extension along the eastern margin. The empty northern interior is a real absence rather than an absence of observation: the same satellites observed it on the same days. The gradient is steep, spanning roughly two orders of magnitude between the peat belt and the northern interior, which means resource allocation proportional to intensity would be very unevenly distributed. That is the operational content of a first-order surface, and it is the strongest planning-relevant thing my first-order analysis alone supports.





I also computed an adaptive estimator as a check, because a fixed bandwidth over-smooths sparse areas and under-smooths dense ones. It reproduces the same principal concentration, which is the reassurance I was after: the structure I report is not an artefact of forcing one bandwidth everywhere.

Figure 9: Nearest-neighbour G, empty-space F, and the centred L function, each against a complete spatial randomness envelope from 199 simulations. What I take from it: every statistic departs from the CSR envelope immediately and by an enormous margin. G rises far faster than expected, meaning nearest neighbours are much closer than random; F rises far slower, meaning empty gaps are much larger than random; L sits far above zero at every lag. Read naively this is overwhelming evidence of clustering. Read correctly it is evidence of almost nothing, because the sensor guarantees this result: a single fire produces adjacent detections. I include it to make that failure visible rather than hide it. The analysis I actually rely on is in Section 7.3.

section: 7.6 Extending the range, after getting it wrong
text:
7.6 Extending the range, after getting it wrong
I set the 5 km cap because long lags in an elongated window rest on few pairs. That reasoning is fine, but 5 km was more conservative than I needed. The rule I stated in Section 5 caps \(r\) at a quarter of the window’s shortest dimension, and the window is 86 km wide, so 20 km was admissible the whole time. Extending to 20 km is not me granting myself a post-hoc licence, it is me finally applying the rule I had already written down.
Two practical constraints came with that, and I am disclosing both rather than hiding them. pcfinhom offers no border correction, and the translation correction over roughly seven million pairs per pattern would not finish in a workable time for 99 simulated patterns. So my significance across the extended range rests on \(L_{inhom}\) with a border correction and a full envelope, while the shape of \(g_{inhom}\) comes from a single translation-corrected curve with no simulations. I make no significance claim for \(g_{inhom}\) beyond 3 km.

                             panel = "L_inhom(r) - r, with envelope")

  transmute(r, obs = trans, lo = NA_real_, hi = NA_real_, ref = 1,
            panel = "g_inhom(r), observed only")
ggplot(bind_rows(Lx, Gx), aes(r)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.75, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_line(aes(y = ref), colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(aes(y = obs), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +

  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  labs(x = "r", y = NULL,

       subtitle = glue("Dotted line marks {round(EX$summary_ext$r_g_within_10pct_of_1/1000, 1)} km, where g_inhom first comes within 10% of 1.")) +
  theme_ex01(base_size = 9)








Figure 14: Left, inhomogeneous centred L function to 20 km with a 99-simulation envelope. Right, the observed inhomogeneous pair correlation function over the same range, with no envelope, on a log scale. What I take from it: the two panels answer different questions and disagree in an instructive way. g_inhom, which localises scale, peaks at about 440 m and decays steadily: it is 4.3 at 1 km, 2.7 at 2 km, 1.4 at 5 km, and reaches within 10% of its asymptote of 1 at about 7.2 km. L_inhom, which is cumulative, never re-enters its envelope within 20 km. Both are correct. The excess pair density is a local phenomenon that has largely dissipated by 7 km, and because L accumulates every excess at smaller lags it remains significantly elevated far beyond the range over which anything is actually happening.

I cross-checked the extended curve against my Section 7.3 estimate over the lags both cover, since both use the translation correction. The median relative difference is 0.15%, so changing the \(r\) grid has not quietly changed the estimate underneath me.
So here is my corrected answer to Q3. Residual clustering begins immediately above the sensor floor, is strongest at roughly 438 m, and only decays to within 10% of no excess by about 7.2 km. title: Where peat burns, and how close together
text:
11.2 Where my analysis is weakest
Four places, roughly in order of how much they worry me.
My event definition does the heavy lifting. Collapsing detections to cells is defensible and I think necessary, but it is a modelling decision that I have presented as data preparation, and I should be honest that those are not the same thing. A cell that burned for three weeks and a cell that burned for one overpass contribute identically to ppp_cell. If I weighted cells by persistence or by cumulative radiative power I would be answering a related but different question, and I am not certain I would reach the same conclusion about scale.
My inhomogeneous null is estimated from the data I am testing. The bias runs in the conservative direction, so I am comfortable that the rejection stands. But the magnitude of the excess clustering is not reliably estimated, so anything I say about how much clustering there is should be read as ordinal rather than quantitative.
Detectability is confounded with intensity. I cannot discharge assumptions A1 and A2 within this data source. Sub-surface peat smouldering, the mode I care most about for public health, is systematically under-detected, and cloud cover is not plausibly independent of location. What I have mapped is a surface of detected fire, not of fire.
One of my decisions was simply wrong and I had to reverse it. I initially capped the r range at 5 km. Every inhomogeneous statistic sat outside its envelope across the whole of that range, which means my cap could not answer the question I set it to answer, and my first draft drew a conclusion from it that the extended analysis contradicts. I have left the cap in the record rather than quietly replacing it. A range chosen before seeing the curves and then revised when the curves demanded it is a different thing from a range chosen to produce a tidy answer, and a reader has no way to tell those apart unless I say which one happened.

title: Global Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
1. Overview
Exercise 4 built the weights matrix. This exercise finally uses it to answer a question worth asking: is Hunan’s economic development spatially clustered, or is it scattered at random across the province?
That matters because the two cases call for different policy. If wealthy counties are scattered, each one succeeded on its own terms and there is little to generalise. If they are clustered, something is spilling across county borders, and the unit of intervention is the region rather than the county.
The techniques split into two levels:

Global measures return one number for the whole map. Moran’s I and Geary’s C answer “is there clustering anywhere”.
Local measures return one number per county. LISA and Getis-Ord Gi* answer “clustering where”, which is the question a planner actually has.

I expected the local maps to be a more detailed version of the global result. They are not, and the gap between them turned out to be the most useful thing in this exercise.

5. Visualising the Distribution
Before any test, look at the map. A statistic that disagrees with the picture usually means the statistic was computed wrong.

equal <- tm_shape(hunan) +
  tm_polygons("GDPPC", fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(n = 5, style = "equal"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Equal interval")) +
  tm_borders(col_alpha = 0.5)

  tm_polygons("GDPPC", fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(n = 5, style = "quantile"),

NoteThe two classifications disagree about how many rich counties there are



Equal interval puts almost every county in the bottom class, because Changsha at 88,656 stretches the range so far that the other 87 counties are squeezed together. Equal quantile forces 20% into each class and shows a north-east cluster clearly.
Neither is wrong. Equal interval is honest about the magnitude of the gap; quantile is honest about the ranking. The reason this matters for the rest of the exercise is that Moran’s I works on deviations from the mean, and that mean of 24,405 is dragged upward by a handful of counties. Most of Hunan sits below its own provincial average.

6.2 Moran’s I Test

moran.test(hunan$GDPPC, listw = rswm_q, zero.policy = TRUE, na.action = na.omit)


    Moran I test under randomisation

data:  hunan$GDPPC  
weights: rswm_q    

Moran I statistic standard deviate = 4.7351, p-value = 1.095e-06
alternative hypothesis: greater
sample estimates:

      0.300749970      -0.011494253       0.004348351 


Moran’s I is 0.3007 against an expected value of -0.0115 under spatial randomness. The z-score is 4.735 and p is about 1.1e-06.
So: positive spatial autocorrelation. Counties resemble their neighbours more than chance would produce. On the standard reading of Moran’s I, which runs roughly -1 to +1, 0.30 is moderate rather than overwhelming.


6.3 Monte Carlo Moran’s I
The analytical p-value assumes normality, and GDPPC is clearly skewed. A permutation test avoids that assumption entirely by shuffling the values across counties 999 times and asking where the observed value falls.

set.seed(1234)
bperm <- moran.mc(hunan$GDPPC, listw = rswm_q, nsim = 999, zero.policy = TRUE, na.action = na.omit)
bperm


    Monte-Carlo simulation of Moran I

data:  hunan$GDPPC 
weights: rswm_q  
number of simulations + 1: 1000 

statistic = 0.30075, observed rank = 1000, p-value = 0.001
alternative hypothesis: greater


The observed statistic ranks 1000 out of 1000, giving p = 0.001. No permutation of the data produced clustering as strong as the real arrangement. The conclusion survives dropping the normality assumption, which is the point of running it.


6.4 Visualising the Simulation

     main = "999 permutations against the observed value")

The simulated distribution sits around zero, as it should when values are scattered at random. The observed value sits outside the whole distribution.


6.5 Geary’s C Test

geary.test(hunan$GDPPC, listw = rswm_q)


    Geary C test under randomisation

data:  hunan$GDPPC 
weights: rswm_q   

Geary C statistic standard deviate = 3.6108, p-value = 0.0001526

sample estimates:
Geary C statistic       Expectation          Variance 
        0.6907223         1.0000000         0.0073364 


Geary’s C is 0.6907 against an expected 1. Values below 1 indicate positive autocorrelation, so this agrees with Moran’s I.


6.6 Monte Carlo Geary’s C

set.seed(1234)
bperm_geary <- geary.mc(hunan$GDPPC, listw = rswm_q, nsim = 999)
bperm_geary


    Monte-Carlo simulation of Geary C

data:  hunan$GDPPC 
weights: rswm_q  
number of simulations + 1: 1000 

statistic = 0.69072, observed rank = 1, p-value = 0.001
alternative hypothesis: greater


p = 0.001 again.






NoteWhy run both when they agree



Moran’s I is built on cross-products of deviations from the global mean, so it responds to the overall pattern. Geary’s C is built on squared differences between neighbouring pairs, so it is more sensitive to local differences between adjacent units.
When they agree, as here, the reading is that the pattern is not an artefact of one formulation. If Moran’s I had come back positive while Geary’s C indicated no structure, that would have pointed to a broad regional gradient without sharp neighbour-to-neighbour similarity, and would have been worth chasing. Agreement is the boring outcome, but it is only boring because it was checked.

I expected the correlation to decay toward zero as lag increases, and it does through lag 4. What I did not expect is that it goes negative at lags 5 and 6.
Decay to zero would mean influence simply fades with distance. Going negative means something stronger: counties five or six steps apart are systematically dissimilar. section: 8. Additional Exploration: Does the Choice of Weights Change Moran’s I?
text:
8. Additional Exploration: Does the Choice of Weights Change Moran’s I?
Everything above used queen contiguity. Exercise 4 built four different weighting schemes, and I was left wondering how much of Moran’s I is the data and how much is the matrix.
First the distance-based neighbours, which need a cut-off large enough that no county is left isolated.

coords <- st_coordinates(st_centroid(st_geometry(hunan)))
k1 <- knn2nb(knearneigh(coords))
dmax <- max(unlist(nbdists(k1, coords, longlat = TRUE)))
round(dmax, 2)

[1] 61.81








WarningPass coordinates, not geometry



My first attempt passed st_centroid() output straight into knearneigh(), an sfc object rather than a coordinate matrix, and the maximum first-neighbour distance came back as 0.60 instead of 61.81. The longlat = TRUE argument is silently ignored, so spdep measures in degrees as though they were planar units.
It does not error. It produces a perfectly well-formed weights matrix that is completely wrong. I made this exact mistake in Exercise 4, wrote it up, and made it again here. What saved me was the habit the first one left behind: look at the number and ask whether 0.6 km is plausible for Chinese counties.


Now the four schemes.

d62 <- dnearneigh(coords, 0, dmax, longlat = TRUE)
wm_r <- poly2nb(hunan, queen = FALSE)
k6 <- knn2nb(knearneigh(coords, k = 6))
schemes <- list(Queen = wm_q, Rook = wm_r, `knn (k=6)` = k6, `Fixed 62km` = d62)

map_dfr(names(schemes), function(nm) {
  lw <- nb2listw(schemes[[nm]], style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)
  m <- moran.test(hunan$GDPPC, lw, zero.policy = TRUE)
  tibble(Scheme = nm,
         `Avg neighbours` = round(mean(card(schemes[[nm]])), 2),
         `Moran's I` = round(unname(m$estimate[1]), 4),
         z = round(unname(m$statistic), 3),
         p = format.pval(m$p.value, digits = 3))
}) %>% kable()

title: Global Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
9. What I Take Away
Hunan’s development is spatially clustered, and the evidence is not marginal. Moran’s I of 0.3007 against an expected -0.0115 gives z = 4.735 and p near 1e-06, and the permutation test puts the observed value outside all 999 simulations. Geary’s C agrees from a different formulation. The conclusion survives dropping the normality assumption, which is the reason to run the Monte Carlo version at all.
The correlogram’s negative tail was worth plotting. Decay to zero would mean influence simply fades with distance. Turning negative at lags 5 and 6 means counties that far apart are systematically dissimilar, which is the signature of a core and a periphery rather than a smooth gradient. The boundary is crossed at about four steps.
The direction is robust, the magnitude is not. Moran’s I moves between 0.30 and 0.42 across four reasonable weighting schemes. Reporting the number without naming the matrix that produced it would not be reproducible. Fewer and nearer neighbours means a higher index, every time.
And a global statistic is an average over the whole map. It says clustering exists somewhere. It cannot say where, it cannot say whether the clustering is in the rich counties or the poor ones, and it cannot say how much of the province participates. Part 02 takes the same data apart county by county, and the answer turns out to be narrower than this number suggests.

title: Local Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
1. Overview
Part 01 established that Hunan’s GDP per capita is spatially clustered: Moran’s I of 0.3007 with p near 1e-06. That is one number for 88 counties, and it cannot say where the clustering is.
This part decomposes it. Local Moran’s I (LISA) returns a statistic per county and classifies each into high-high, low-low, high-low or low-high. Getis-Ord Gi* asks a different question again: is this neighbourhood’s total unusually high or low?
I expected the local maps to be a more detailed version of the global result. They are not, and the gap between them is the most useful thing here. I also found an error in the reference code along the way, and it inverted the finding.

The second axis in that code is LM_I, the local Moran statistic itself. That cannot work, and the reason is in the formula. Local Moran’s I for county i is

section: 4. Hot and Cold Spot Analysis with Getis-Ord Gi*
text:
4. Hot and Cold Spot Analysis with Getis-Ord Gi*
LISA asks whether a county resembles its neighbours. Gi* asks whether a neighbourhood’s total is unusually high or low, and answers in z-score units.

4.1 Deriving the Weights

coords <- st_coordinates(st_centroid(st_geometry(hunan)))
k1 <- knn2nb(knearneigh(coords))
k1dists <- unlist(nbdists(k1, coords, longlat = TRUE))
summary(k1dists)

  24.79   32.56   38.00   39.07   44.52   61.81 








WarningI walked into the same trap I documented last exercise



My first run passed st_centroid() output straight into knearneigh() and got a maximum first-neighbour distance of 0.60 instead of 61.81. That is the exact sfc versus coordinate-matrix mistake I wrote a callout about in Exercise 4, and I made it again within a fortnight.
Writing the lesson down was evidently not the same as learning it. What saved me was the habit the last one left behind: I looked at the number, knew 0.6 km was impossible for Chinese counties, and checked. The value of documenting a mistake was not that I stopped making it, but that I now recognise the symptom on sight.


Maximum first-nearest-neighbour distance is 61.81 km, the cut-off that guarantees every county at least one neighbour.


4.2 Gi* with Fixed Distance Weights
Gi* includes the county itself, which is what include.self() is for and what the star in the name denotes.

gi.fixed <- localG(hunan$GDPPC, nb2listw(include.self(d62), style = "B"))

  rename(gstat_fixed = as.matrix.gi.fixed.)

The fixed-distance scheme finds 7 hot spots and 0 cold spots. The adaptive scheme finds 15 hot spots and 5 cold spots. Same variable, same province, same threshold.
The mechanism is the neighbour count. The fixed 62 km band averages 3.64 neighbours, and in the sparse western counties it gives very few. A Gi* z-score built from three units cannot reach far from zero, so the poor west never crosses -2. Forcing k = 8 gives those same counties a wider window, their deficit accumulates over more neighbours, and cold spots appear.
Pingjiang makes the point sharply. Its GDPPC is 17,252, below the provincial median of 20,433, so it is a genuinely poor county. Under the fixed band its Gi* is +1.95; under adaptive k = 8 it is +4.61, which would be reported as a strong hot spot. The corrected LISA classifies it as low-high, a poor county surrounded by wealth, which is the honest description.
“Hunan has no economic cold spots” is a sentence I could have written from the fixed-band map alone, and it would have been an artefact of the neighbour definition. Report the weights with the result, every time.

title: Local Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
5. What I Take Away
I caught a real error in the reference code, and only because I checked the output against the data. The chapter’s quadrant assignment uses local Moran’s I as an axis, and because that statistic is positive for high-high and low-low alike, it cannot separate them. Five of 11 significant counties were mislabelled, low-low was reported as empty when there are two, and three spurious high-low counties appeared. Running the code and mapping the result would have shown nothing wrong. Reading one row against its own values did.
The wrong answer was the more interesting one. “Hunan has no low-low clusters at all” is a better line than “seven high-high against two low-low”, and I had already written it. Findings that flatter the analysis deserve more scepticism than findings that complicate it, not less.
Global and local measures answer different questions. Part 01’s Moran’s I of 0.30 at p near 1e-06 sounds province-wide. Locally, 77 of 88 counties are indistinguishable from random and the pattern is carried by a minority around Changsha. A significant global statistic does not mean most places participate.
Two statistics can both be right and disagree. Xiangyin is 13th by GDPPC and 3rd by Gi*, and insignificant under LISA. Neither is broken; Gi* scores the neighbourhood and LISA scores the county against its neighbours. The choice belongs to the question being asked.
Weights are not a preliminary step. Whether Hunan has any cold spots at all flips between 0 and 5 on the neighbour definition alone. Exercise 4 presented weights as setup for the real analysis. They are part of the result.
And I repeated a documented mistake. The sfc versus coordinate-matrix trap cost me time in Exercise 4, I wrote it up carefully, and I made it again here. What had stuck was the sanity check rather than the rule, which is probably the realistic version of learning from a mistake.

title: Emerging Hot Spot Analysis
text:
1. Overview
Exercise 5 found a hot spot around Changsha in 2012. It could not say whether that hot spot was new, fading, or permanent, because it only ever saw one year.
Emerging Hot Spot Analysis adds the time axis. It computes Gi* for every location in every time period, then runs a Mann-Kendall trend test on each location’s sequence of Gi* values, and classifies the result into categories such as persistent, intensifying, diminishing, sporadic and oscillating.
The question this answers is the one a planner actually cares about: not “where is it hot” but “where is it becoming hot”.
I will say at the outset that the headline result of this exercise is a bug I found in the sfdep package rather than a fact about Hunan. The fact about Hunan only became visible after fixing it.

5. Creating a Space-Time Cube
A spacetime cube pairs each location with each time period. sfdep validates that the pairing is complete, which is why the balanced-panel check above mattered.

6. Computing Gi* Year by Year
First derive the neighbours and weights, then compute Gi* within each year.

GDPPC_nb <- GDPPC_st %>%
  activate("geometry") %>%
  mutate(nb = include_self(st_contiguity(geometry)),
         wt = st_inverse_distance(nb, geometry, scale = 1, alpha = 1),
         .before = 1) %>%
  set_nbs("nb") %>%
  set_wts("wt")


gi_stars <- GDPPC_nb %>%
  group_by(Year) %>%
  mutate(gi = local_gstar_perm(GDPPC, nb, wt, nsim = 99)) %>%
  tidyr::unnest(gi) %>%
  ungroup()


gi_stars %>%
  group_by(Year) %>%
  summarise(Hot = sum(gi_star > 2), Cold = sum(gi_star < -2)) %>%
  pivot_longer(-Year) %>%
  ggplot(aes(Year, value, colour = name)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) + geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Hot = "#C0392B", Cold = "#2c7bb6")) +

title: Emerging Hot Spot Analysis
text:
11. What I Take Away
Three exercises, three silent failures, and none of them threw an error. The sfc coordinate trap in Exercise 4, the quadrant axis error in Exercise 5, and now an ordering mismatch inside a published CRAN package. Every one produced output of the correct shape and plausible appearance. The only thing that caught any of them was checking a result against the values it claimed to describe.
The check that works is cheap and always the same. Join the output back to the input and ask whether it is consistent. Counties called hot spots should have high Gi*. That took one line and four seconds, and it is the difference between this exercise and a confidently wrong map.
Trusting a package is not the same as trusting a result. sfdep is on CRAN, is written by a competent author, and implements all seventeen ArcGIS EHSA classes correctly. The classification logic is fine. One cbind at the end attaches it to the wrong rows. A package being good is not evidence that a particular call to it returned what you think.
The bug is invisible on data that happens to be sorted. If Hunan’s shapefile had stored its counties alphabetically, this code would be correct and I would have found nothing. Whether an analysis is right would then depend on the storage order of a file nobody looks at. That is worth remembering when a workflow “works on my machine”.
On Hunan itself: the Changsha corridor is not an emerging hot spot, it is a permanent one, hot in all seventeen years and already established before the data begins. The change is happening in a ring of middle-income counties to its north whose relative standing is rising, and in a western periphery that has become more tightly clustered in its disadvantage. Growth of 6.7 times province-wide moved the levels and left the structure almost exactly as it found it.

It does not overturn any second-order result. The clustering scale, the Knox interaction and the covariate relationships are all estimated within 2026 and stand on their own.
It changes the interpretation of every one of them. I had been describing the spatial structure of a dry season. I was in fact describing the spatial structure of a severe dry season, one of the two worst in the fourteen-year record. A cluster scale of about a kilometre, and a containment window of days, are properties measured under extreme conditions. Whether they hold in a median year, where the regency records a few dozen burned cells rather than eight thousand, is not something this analysis can tell you, and there may be too few events in a median year to estimate them at all.
That is a more useful limitation than the one it replaces, because it is specific.

6. Two nulls: one meaningless, one that can fail













Against CSR, G, F and L all leave the envelope immediately. That persuades nobody, including me: the sensor guarantees it. g(r) is even suppressed below 375 m, which is the pixel, not fires avoiding each other.
So I changed the null. An inhomogeneous Poisson process with intensity from the 4 km kernel estimate, with the reference re-estimated for every simulated pattern. Everything my first-order analysis found is already inside it.
The departure survives. Both global tests reject at the Monte Carlo floor.
The two panels disagree, and that was the lesson. L_inhom never re-enters its envelope in 20 km; g_inhom, which localises scale, peaks at 438 m and is within 10% of no-excess by 7.2 km. My first draft capped r at 5 km and drew the wrong conclusion from exactly this.

7.4 Testing isotropy, instead of just assuming it
Assumption A7 says \(K\), \(L\) and \(g\) all average over direction, and that I expected real anisotropy because peat fires spread with the wind and along canal lines. Listing an assumption and never testing it is the kind of thing that should not survive a read, so this section tests it. The test found something, but not the thing I predicted, and the first version of my own analysis missed it.
Why I did not use the packaged tools. spatstat offers Ksector and pairorient, and neither accepts a lambda argument: both assume homogeneity. Applied here they would reject isotropy for two reasons that have nothing to do with fire. The window is 86 km wide and 213 km tall, so even a perfectly isotropic process yields more north-south pairs than east-west ones purely because there is more room that way. And intensity is concentrated in a south-southeast band, so any pair drawn from inside it inherits that elongation.
I therefore built the null the way I built it for clustering: simulate from an inhomogeneous Poisson process with the same \(\hat{\lambda}\) from Section 6, which absorbs the window geometry and the first-order trend together.
Two statistics, and the second one is the point. Orientations here are axial, so I double the angles before averaging and summarise concentration by the mean resultant length \(R_2 = |n^{-1}\sum_k e^{2i\theta_k}|\), which is 0 when orientations are spread evenly and 1 when every pair lies on one axis.
Each harmonic is blind to the next one up, and I walked into that twice.
\(R_2\) detects a single preferred axis and is structurally blind to four-fold structure, because a rose with spikes at 0 and 90 degrees has its doubled angles cancel. My first version of this section reported the short range as isotropic on the strength of \(R_2\) alone, and the rose diagram contradicted it on sight. So I added \(R_4 = |n^{-1}\sum_k e^{4i\theta_k}|\).
\(R_4\) is in turn blind to eight-fold structure. Spikes at 0, 45, 90 and 135 degrees have a 45-degree period, so under \(e^{4i\theta}\) the 45 and 135 pair sits in antiphase to the 0 and 90 pair and the two cancel. That is exactly the shape a square grid produces, because a lattice offers displacements along its axes and along its diagonals. \(R_8\) is what captures it, and it turns out to be the largest directional signal anywhere in this analysis.
The general lesson is worth stating plainly, because it cost me two passes: a harmonic statistic only finds the structure you asked it about, and the way to avoid missing the rest is to look at the rose.

7.4.1 The short-range structure is my grid, and the sensor’s
Over 375 to 750 m the eight-fold concentration is 0.087 against 0.007 under the null, < 0.005. That is more than twelve times the null value and the largest directional effect measured anywhere in this report. The four-fold term is 0.0289, also significant, and \(R_2\) is 0.0063 against a null of 0.0066, 0.475, which is nothing at all.
Three statistics on the same 36,860 pairs, and they disagree completely. The structure is spikes on the axes and on the diagonals, which is what a square lattice produces and what only the eighth harmonic can see.
My first explanation was that this is entirely my own doing. ppp_cell keeps at most one point per 375 m cell, so short-range displacements are dominated by lattice vectors: 375 m at 0 and 90 degrees, 530 m on the diagonals, 750 m at two cells. That would produce spikes exactly where they appear. The way to check it is to run the identical test on ppp_all, which keeps every detection at its own sensor coordinate and has no such lattice.

7.4.2 At longer range, a real but negligible tilt
From 750 m outward every harmonic goes quiet. Over 750 to 1500 m, \(R_4\) is 9^{-4} (0.930) and \(R_8\) is 0.0021 (0.665), both below their nulls. That is what a lattice explanation predicts, since every lattice vector is shorter than 750 m, and it is the check that makes me believe the short-range result is geometric rather than physical.
What remains is a weak single-axis elongation that grows with distance, reaching \(R_2 =\) 0.024 over 3000 to 6000 m against a null of 0.0055. That is statistically distinguishable at the Monte Carlo floor and it is 2.4% of the way to perfect alignment, which is not a directional pattern in any sense a fire officer would recognise.

7.4.4 What this changes
A7 is now tested rather than asserted, and every part of what I originally wrote turns out to be wrong. I said anisotropy was likely because fires follow canals, and that it would make my clustering estimates conservative.
The directional structure that exists at short range is geometric, not meteorological. It comes from the 375 m cell grid and from the sensor’s own scan grid, not from wind or canals. Beyond 750 m, where the clustering actually lives, no harmonic finds anything, so the isotropic \(K\), \(L\) and \(g\) are estimating what they claim to and there is no conservatism to claim on those grounds.
One practical consequence for the rest of the report. Because the eight-fold structure is symmetric about the cardinal axes and the diagonals, it very largely cancels in any statistic that averages over direction, which is what \(K\), \(L\) and \(g\) do. So it does not bias the clustering results. It would wreck a directional analysis, and anyone extending this work should thin differently before attempting one.
